true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
downsize method is redefined, silently dropping the 4-arg overload

The patch keeps the original `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` on line 145 and then defines a second `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` on line 149. In Ruby, the later definition replaces the earlier one entirely; the first signature no longer accepts calls. Any existing caller that invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height)` (4 positional args) will now raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments`. The resize/downsize helpers are used by jobs and other models, so this is a silent breaking change. Either keep a single canonical signature and migrate all callers, or branch inside one method based on argument types.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size check ignores site-configured limits

`validateUploadedFile` used to read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB regardless of site settings or file type. This means admins who set a tighter limit (e.g. 3 MB) will accept up to 10 MB in the browser, only to be rejected by the server (or worse, accepted via the new auto-downsize path on the server). The client and server limits should stay aligned through the same setting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message reports a hardcoded 10 MB instead of configured max_image_size_kb

`displayErrorForUpload` previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the user-facing alert, so the message matched the admin-configured limit. After the change it always says 10 MB. Users whose site has a lower (or higher) configured `max_image_size_kb` will see a misleading error string, which makes support and self-service diagnosis harder.

Comment claims automatic reduction 'to allowed size' but loop only shrinks by 20%

The comment '# allow users to upload large images that will be automatically reduced to allowed size' implies the file will end up under `max_image_size_kb`. As noted above, 5 iterations of 80% scaling often cannot reach the configured byte limit, so users can still hit 'file too large' rejections. The comment also conflates pixel-dimension reduction with byte-size reduction, which can mislead future maintainers. Either tighten the algorithm so the promise holds, or rephrase the comment to reflect what the loop actually does.

Downsize failure is ignored, looping on the same oversized file

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns `false` (and logs an error) when ImageMagick fails, but the controller loop does not check the return value. On failure the underlying file is unchanged, so `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` stays true and the loop spins through all 5 attempts invoking `convert` again on the same broken file. The loop should break as soon as `downsize` reports failure, and ideally propagate a clear error to the user instead of silently accepting an over-limit upload.

Downsize loop may not bring the image under max_image_size_kb

The retry loop scales the image to 80% of its current dimensions up to 5 times. Five iterations of 0.8x only reduces dimensions to ~0.328x of the original, which for typical JPEG/PNG content yields a file that is often larger than 32.7% of the original size. If the input is much bigger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (e.g. 20 MB uploaded against a 1 MB limit) the loop exits with `attempt == 0` and `tempfile.size` still > the limit. `Upload.create_for` is then called with an oversized file, which either fails with a confusing error or, if server-side validation is lenient, succeeds with a file violating the configured policy. The loop should compare the actual byte size to the limit and either grow the reduction factor, use binary search on the quality/scale, or surface a clear error when the target cannot be reached.

URL download limit is hardcoded to 10 MB regardless of max_image_size_kb

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was changed to `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. This decouples the maximum downloadable remote upload from the configured `max_image_size_kb` (which can be 1 MB, 5 MB, or unlimited). On installations with a tight policy, a remote URL can now fetch up to 10 MB and then attempt to downsize; on installations that set a higher limit, downloads above the configured limit are still capped at 10 MB. Either keep using the setting (and let the downsize loop handle oversize) or document the deliberate cap.

convert_with executes a shell string built from interpolated arguments

`convert_with` runs `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``, joining instruction-array entries with spaces and passing the result to the shell. With the refactor, `dimensions` is now passed as a free-form string (e.g. `"80%"`) from `OptimizedImage.downsize`'s third argument, and the controller already passes such a string. Any future caller that forwards user-controlled content into `dimensions` (or into `from`/`to` paths) can inject shell metacharacters and achieve command execution as the Rails process. The code should use the array form (e.g. `system(*instructions, out: '/dev/null', err: '/dev/null')`) so each argument is passed directly to `execve` without a shell.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
save_host dereferences params[:embeddable_host] without guarding against missing/nested keys

`host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `host.category_id = params[:embeddable_host][:category_id]` will raise KeyError if the `:embeddable_host` key is absent (e.g., a client POSTs empty form-data) or NoMethodError if it is nil. The subsequent `self.host.sub!` in `before_validation` also crashes when `host` is nil. Use strong parameters and defensive parsing (e.g., `(params[:embeddable_host] || {}).fetch(:host, nil)`) so the controller renders a 400 instead of a 500.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update action crashes with NoMethodError when the requested host does not exist

`EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` can return nil if the id is missing, but `save_host(nil)` then executes `nil.host = ...`, raising NoMethodError and returning 500 to the admin. The destroy action has the same problem at line 15. Use `find_by(id: params[:id])` and short-circuit with a 404 / `not_found` when the record is missing instead of passing nil into save_host / calling destroy on nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
record_for_host comparison fails for hosts with any uppercase characters

`URI(host).host` preserves the case of the hostname. The query `where("lower(host) = ?", host).first` lowercases the DB column but leaves the parameter unchanged. If a URL's host is `EXAMPLE.com`, `lower("example.com")` (column) does not equal `"EXAMPLE.com"` (parameter) and no record is found, so the host is rejected even though a matching record exists (e.g., Browser sent Referer with uppercase letters, which is not normalized by the Rack referer middleware). Lowercase the parameter: `where("lower(host) = ?", host.downcase).first`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents are swapped between category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb

The PR moves the existing `Fabricator(:category)` block into the new `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` and adds `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` to `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb`. The two files end up with swapped contents. Fabrication still works (it autoloads every file in the directory), but the next person to read these files will be confused and will edit the wrong one. Restore the canonical layout: put the category fabricator in `category_fabricator.rb` and the embeddable_host one in `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL injection in migration via interpolated host value

The migration inserts into embeddable_hosts using string interpolation: VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...). The value of h comes from the legacy embeddable_hosts site setting (one per line) and is used unescaped. A value containing a single quote (or other SQL meta-characters) would either break the migration or, if the site setting was modified outside of Rails, allow arbitrary SQL execution during migrate. Use parameterized SQL (e.g., ActiveRecord::Base.connection.exec_query with a bound host, or a model.create!) instead of string interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category / uncategorized_category_id settings are missing

The query `SELECT c.id FROM categories c INNER JOIN site_settings s ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'` returns zero rows if either site setting has never been set, and `[0]['id']` on an empty result raises. The same pattern is used on line 15 for `uncategorized_category_id`. Either setting being missing aborts the migration entirely, leaving the deploy in a half-migrated state. Guard with a count check (e.g., `result.any? ? result[0]['id'].to_i : nil`) or look up via the SiteSetting/Category models instead of raw SQL.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
Admin::EmbeddableHostsController spec only asserts class inheritance, not behavior

The single test is `expect(Admin::EmbeddableHostsController < Admin::AdminController).to eq(true)`. There is no coverage for the create / update / destroy actions, for normalization of the host (stripping http(s) and path), for the uncategorized fallback when category_id is blank, for rejecting hosts that fail the format regex, or for the nil-when-id-missing case. After fixing the bugs above, add specs that exercise these flows. `spec/controllers/admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb` has the same issue (single inheritance test).

EmbeddingSerializer uses embed: :ids which prevents hydration of nested embeddable_hosts in the admin client

The serializer declares `has_many :embeddable_hosts, serializer: EmbeddableHostSerializer, embed: :ids`. With `embed: :ids` the JSON payload only contains `embeddable_host_ids: [...]` in the embedding object, but no separate top-level `embeddable_hosts` array. The store's `_hydrateEmbedded` requires the pluralized array to be present in the root to look up and hydrate objects from the IDs. As a result, the admin embedding page will always show an empty table even when embeddable hosts exist. Change to `embed: :objects` (or omit the embed option) so the full embeddable_hosts array is included in the response.

Focus observer fires when editing toggles from true to false, leaking focus to the read-only host-name

`_focusOnInput` is decorated with both `@on('didInsertElement')` and `@observes('editing')`, so it runs whenever `editing` changes. After Cancel sets `editToggled` to false, the observer schedules `this.$('.host-name').focus()` for `afterRender`. Because the input is inside `{{#if editing}}`, that selector does not exist in the rendered DOM, so on some browsers the focus falls back to body and subsequent keypresses after Cancel can land outside the component. Guard the body with `if (this.get('editing'))` before scheduling the focus.

Migration silently inserts category_id = 0 when uncategorized_category_id is missing

When the embed_category lookup yields nothing and the uncategorized fallback also returns nothing, `category_id` is left at 0 (or set to `-1` if `uncategorized_category_id` is still at its YAML default). Rows are then INSERTed with category_id = 0/-1, violating no DB constraint but creating data whose `belongs_to :category` association is permanently broken and which will never pass `belongs_to` validation on any future save (including admin edits). The migration should either abort in that case or skip the host with a warning.

category_id has no foreign key or index, allowing dangling references and inefficient lookups

The migration declares `t.integer :category_id, null: false` with no FK constraint and no index. Without an FK, deleting a category leaves `embeddable_hosts` with dangling `category_id` values that break the association. Also the lookup `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` performs a sequential scan; an index (ideally functional, `lower(host)`) would make `record_for_host` scale. Add `add_foreign_key :embeddable_hosts, :categories` (and a unique/functional index on host) before relying on this in production.

store#update passes a callback that the REST adapter never invokes

`update(type, id, attrs)` calls `this.adapterFor(type).update(this, type, id, attrs, function(result) { ... storeMap ... return result; })`, but the RestAdapter's `update` signature only accepts four arguments and ignores any callback. The closure that re-keys the identity map when the server reassigns the id is therefore dead code: after a PUT that returns a new id, the store keeps the record under the old id in `_identityMap`. Either extend the adapter to invoke the callback, or drop the dead code to avoid future confusion.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when no TopicUser row exists

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(...)` may return nil if the current user has no TopicUser record for that topic (e.g. they have never visited it). The very next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`, which will raise `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil`. The action needs to handle the nil case, e.g. create the row or short-circuit, otherwise every unsubscribe from a never-visited topic raises a 500.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in controller property name and template binding

The property is defined as `stopNotificiationsText` (note the doubled 'i') and is consumed by the template as `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}`. While the template still resolves because both sides share the typo, this will trip future readers and any future rename attempt. The i18n key (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`) is correctly spelled, so the property should be `stopNotificationsText`.

false_positives.candidate:
Bypasses TopicUser.change side effects

The action writes the new notification level with `tu.save!`, instead of using `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)`. As a result `notifications_changed_at`, `notifications_reason_id`, and the `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` message that the rest of the app relies on are skipped. The client will not refresh its notification-level badge, and auditing/debugging of why a notification level changed is lost.

CSRF: GET request mutates notification state

The `unsubscribe` action is wired to two GET routes (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb) and immediately mutates the user's `TopicUser.notification_level` based on `current_user.id`. Rails does not require a CSRF token for GET requests, so any logged-in user can be silently toggled off a topic by an attacker who embeds the unsubscribe URL in an image/link on a third-party site. The unsubscribe URL is also publicly linkable (no signed token), and the `before_filter :ensure_logged_in` does not help because the victim is already authenticated. This should be a POST (or require a signed token like `EmailUnsubscribeKey`), and ideally the state change should happen only after a user gesture.

List-Unsubscribe header ignores topic-specific URL

`header_args` only ever sets `List-Unsubscribe` to `<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>`, even though `@opts[:unsubscribe_url]` is now passed in from `user_notifications.rb`. Email clients use the `List-Unsubscribe` header for one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058); the topic-specific URL the PR just introduced is never used in the header, so the whole point of exposing `unsubscribe_url` to the builder is wasted for header-based unsubscribe.

No authorization / visibility check on topic

Unlike the regular `show` action, `unsubscribe` never calls `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (or any equivalent). `TopicView.new` is invoked with `current_user` but the action then loads/writes a `TopicUser` row for `params[:topic_id]` without verifying the topic exists, is not deleted, and is in a category the user is allowed to see. A user could be subscribed/muted on topics they should never have known about, and the response can leak topic state for topics in restricted categories.

No tests cover the new unsubscribe feature

The PR adds a new controller action, new routes, a new Ember route/controller/view/template, a new `Topic#unsubscribe_url` method, and includes the topic unsubscribe URL in notification emails. The only test change is adding `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to an existing example and asserting `List-Unsubscribe` is present. There are no controller specs for `TopicsController#unsubscribe` (CSRF/POST vs GET, slug redirect, nil TopicUser, permission check), no assertions that the email body actually contains the topic-specific unsubscribe link, and no assertion that `header_args['List-Unsubscribe']` carries the per-topic URL (RFC 8058). Without these the CSRF and behavior regressions above will not be caught.

Template path does not match route registration

The route map registers a top-level route `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' });` and a top-level view `views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, but the template is placed at `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`. Ember resolves templates by dasherizing the route name, so `topicUnsubscribe` looks up `templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs`, not `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` (which would belong to a nested `topic/unsubscribe` route that is not defined). The unsubscribe page will fail to render its body. Either nest the route under `topic` and move the template accordingly, or rename the template/view/controller files so the route, controller, view, and template all use the same `topicUnsubscribe` name.

Unsubscribe toggles instead of muting from email

The toggle logic (`if tu.notification_level > :regular then :regular else :muted`) is appropriate for the on-site notification dropdown, but the link in the email is built via `post.topic.unsubscribe_url` and shown as "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here". A user who is `:tracking` or `:watching` will be downgraded only to `:regular`, not muted, so the unsubscribe email doesn't actually stop notifications on the first click. Either the email link should target an endpoint that always mutes, or the toggle behavior should be reconsidered.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validator has the side effect of writing to blocked_emails

BlockedEmail.should_block? does `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` every time it finds a matching record. It is called from EmailValidator.validate_each, which fires on every User save with `email_changed?` — including profile updates that change an email and any form re-submission that re-validates. As a result match_count and last_match_at are incremented for each validation attempt rather than each actual signup, the validator is no longer idempotent, and a failed DB write inside should_block? raises out of the validator with no rescue (turning a 'blocked email' check into a 500). Statistics should be updated by a separate, explicit call (e.g. in the controller only when the user actually creates an account), and should_block? itself should be a pure check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive email lookup lets users bypass the block list

BlockedEmail.should_block? queries BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first, which is an exact, case-sensitive string match. Email addresses are case-insensitive per RFC 5321, and the User model stores the email as submitted (no downcasing on assignment), so an admin adding `bad@spamclub.com` to blocked_emails will not stop a user signing up with `Bad@SpamClub.com` or `BAD@SPAMCLUB.COM`. Since the entire point of this feature is to reject known-bad addresses, this is a core-functionality bug: the lookup should normalize (downcase and strip) the email before querying, and ideally the BlockedEmail model's uniqueness validation should be made case-insensitive too so admins don't silently end up with duplicate near-spellings.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Domain-setting regex only escapes dots

email_in_restriction_setting? does `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` and feeds the rest directly into Regexp.new. Other regex metacharacters (`*`, `+`, `?`, `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `^`, `$`) in the SiteSetting are interpreted as regex syntax instead of literals, so a value like `mail.ru+` or a multi-domain list with an unexpected separator can match in surprising ways. The legacy code had the same problem, but this is a good opportunity to either escape all regex metacharacters or split the setting on a fixed separator (e.g. `|`) and match each domain literally.

Read-modify-write race on match_count

should_block? loads the record, increments match_count in Ruby, then calls record.save. Two concurrent requests for the same blocked email can each read match_count = N, both increment to N+1, and both save N+1, losing one update. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = NOW()')` or `update_counters`.

Whitelist/blacklist branches of EmailValidator have no tests

The whitelist (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist) and blacklist (SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist) branches were moved out of User#email_validator into the new EmailValidator, but the spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block?. There is no coverage that an email matching the whitelist passes, that a non-whitelisted email gets the :not_allowed error, that a blacklisted email is rejected, or that an existing whitelist/blacklist error suppresses the blocked-email check. Adding tests for those branches would protect against regressions in the moved logic.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin uses full request.referer URL

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` passes the entire referer (including path and query) as the targetOrigin. The browser uses only the origin portion of that string, but cross-origin framing and referrer-policy quirks can produce referer values that are unexpected (e.g. `null`, or some proxied form). The right thing is to compute the origin from `request.referer` in the controller (e.g. via URI) and pass only scheme://host[:port]. Also, no fallback exists when referer is blank, in which case targetOrigin is the empty string and postMessage silently fails to deliver — combined with the embed.js listener's permissive origin check this may surprise integrators.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error

The closing construct is `<%- end if %>`. ERB compiles to Ruby that contains `... end if` at the end of the generated method body. `end` followed by the `if` modifier requires an expression; `end if` with nothing after the `if` (and a `%>` terminator) raises `SyntaxError: unexpected keyword_end`. The view will fail to render whenever it is compiled. Replace with `<%- end %>` (or attach a real condition to the postfix `if`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when RSS item has nil content or title

The body does `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` followed by `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing fields, and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, which crashes the job (`sidekiq_options retry: false`). A single malformed feed item aborts the entire poll, so no later items are imported either. Guard with `i.content.to_s.scrub` (or a presence check) and skip items whose title/link are blank.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Embed iframe is created without a sandbox attribute

The iframe has no `sandbox` (or `allow-scripts`/`allow-same-origin` flags), so the embedded page can run JavaScript with full access to its origin: it can navigate the parent, open popups, send form fields, etc. Even though the embed view is intended to be simple, defense in depth requires `iframe.sandbox = 'allow-scripts allow-same-origin'` (or similar) so that a compromised embed view cannot escalate into the embedder site.

No test for nil/missing RSS fields

The spec only checks the gating SiteSettings. There is no test for poll_feed's handling of an RSS item with no `content` or no `title`, which is what causes the NoMethodError. Add a fixture where the SimpleRSS stub returns an item whose content/title is nil and assert the job completes (or at least skips gracefully).

No test that imported raw_html content is sanitized against XSS

The 'works as expected with a new URL' spec only asserts cooked == raw, which actively cements the unsafe behavior. There is no regression test covering the PollFeed path or import(content containing <script>) that would have caught the stored-XSS issue. Add a fixture whose contents include `<script>alert(1)</script>` and assert the post does not render that script in embed/best.

PollFeed reused without distributed locking

Beyond the synchronous call, even enqueueing PollFeed per retrieval is unsafe because the job body has no distributed lock keyed on the feed URL. With sidekiq concurrency > 1, simultaneous RetrieveTopic jobs would all enqueue PollFeed and they would each import the full feed (TopicEmbed.import is idempotent per embed_url but still does N TopicEmbed.where checks). Use the `feed_key` (declared at the top of poll_feed.rb but never used) as a SETNX-based lock, or rely solely on the scheduled recurrence.

Stored XSS via raw_html cook_method and RSS content

For posts whose cook_method is :raw_html, Post#cook sets cooked equal to raw. The embed view then renders the post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, which outputs the stored content as raw HTML with no escaping. The PollFeed path (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb) calls `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` before passing it into TopicEmbed.import — String#scrub only removes invalid UTF-8 bytes and does NOT strip HTML, so `<script>`, `<iframe>`, etc. from a crafted RSS feed end up stored verbatim and executed in the embed view. The Readability-based import_remote path uses a tag/attribute allow-list, but the RSS path does not. This gives an attacker who can supply a feed (or any party whose source page gets fetched by import_remote without sanitization) a stored XSS that runs in the discourse forum's embed origin.

TopicRetriever runs the full PollFeed job synchronously per retrieval

`perform_retrieve` invokes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` directly. PollFeed is meant to be a Scheduled hourly job that fetches the configured RSS feed and imports all items via TopicEmbed.import. Calling its execute synchronously inside every RetrieveTopic job means each concurrent embed retrieval triggers a full feed fetch + parse + per-item TopicEmbed.import — effectively O(N) feed polls for N concurrent retrievals. Under any non-trivial traffic this hammers the upstream feed and multiplies database writes. The scheduled recurring PollFeed should be left to sidekiq/sidetiq, or TopicRetriever should enqueue PollFeed rather than executing it on the worker thread.

cook_method default of 1 makes every existing post render raw markdown

The migration adds the column with `default: 1`. Post.cook_methods is defined in app/models/post.rb as `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)`, which assigns 0 to :regular and 1 to :raw_html. Post#cook returns raw when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, so every existing post in the database will, after this migration runs, have cooked == raw. The default value should be 0 so legacy posts continue to cook normally; only newly imported RSS/Readability posts (which explicitly set the option in TopicEmbed.import) should be raw_html.

embed_url is never validated against embeddable_host

ensure_embeddable checks that `URI(request.referer).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, but the action then uses the user-supplied `embed_url` parameter to look up `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)` and, when missing, enqueues `RetrieveTopic` for `embed_url`. A caller who can spoof or sit on the embeddable host (any XSS / open redirect there) can query the controller for arbitrary embed URLs and cause RetrieveTopic jobs to fetch arbitrary remote pages reachable to the Discourse server (SSRF). At minimum the controller should reject embed_urls whose host is not embeddable_host; ideally it should compare path/host as well.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! check is outside LOAD_MUTEX

The newly added `ensure_loaded!` does `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` outside any mutex and then calls `load_locale`, which acquires `LOAD_MUTEX`. While `load_locale` re-checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` under the mutex (so correctness is preserved), the outer include check is a TOCTOU pattern: multiple concurrent threads can race past it and redundantly contend on `LOAD_MUTEX`, doing duplicate Array scans and (in the worst case) holding the mutex while reading translation files. The `@loaded_locales ||= []` initialization is also unsynchronized (harmless here since both branches would assign empty arrays). Move the include check inside `LOAD_MUTEX.synchronize` (e.g., inline the load logic) to avoid wasted work under contention.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback ensure_loaded! runs on every request

The new `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` call in `set_locale` runs for every action via the `before_filter`. It allocates a new fallback array via `FallbackLocaleList#[]` on each call and then invokes `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each entry, which performs an unsynchronized `Array#include?` against `@loaded_locales` inside the I18n translation path. For the common case where the user locale equals the default (and `:en` is already loaded), this allocates an array and does redundant checks on a hot path that runs for every request. Consider memoizing the resolved fallback list per locale or skipping the call when all entries are known to be loaded.

FallbackLocaleList extends Hash unnecessarily

`class FallbackLocaleList < Hash` inherits from Hash but the overridden `[]` never reads from Hash storage and no entries are ever written via `store=`/`[]=`. As a result, Hash methods such as `keys`, `values`, `each`, `empty?`, and `fetch` expose the empty underlying Hash state while `[]` returns a generated array — two contradictory views of the same object that will surprise future maintainers. The class also accepts only a single positional `locale`, whereas `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks#[]` accepts splat locales; if any plugin or i18n version ever passes multiple locales here it will raise `ArgumentError`. A plain class (or one whose `[]` takes `*locales`) would be both clearer and safer.

The PR introduces a new `FallbackLocaleList` class with custom `[]` and `ensure_loaded!` methods, deletes the standalone `pluralization.rb` initializer, replaces the default Rails fallback chain, and changes fallback semantics for every translated string on the server — yet no test files appear in the diff. false_positives.candidate:
Docstring and inline comments overstate and misrepresent the feature

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', 'Optimized query path for large datasets'. The `BasePaginator.get_result` comment claims 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' and `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` claims 'permissions are checked at the queryset level'. None of these are true: Django ORM does not silently fix a negative slice (it produces `OFFSET -100` which the DB rejects), no queryset-level permission filter is added in the new code, and no query path is actually optimized. The comments also justify the negative-offset branch with 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', which would be a security/authorization concern if it actually worked. The comments must be rewritten to match what the code does.

No tests added for `OptimizedCursorPaginator`

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class and the modified `BasePaginator.get_result` slicing behavior have no accompanying tests. Cursor-based pagination in this file is subtle (extra row fetching, prev-direction reversal, `cursor.value` dedup, `offset + limit + extra` length check), and the PR introduces a new code path (`enable_advanced_features=True`) plus a behavioral change to the shared `BasePaginator.get_result`. At minimum, tests should cover: (1) forward pagination with the new clamp, (2) backward pagination with positive and negative offsets, (3) the `enable_advanced_features=True` branch with both negative and non-negative offsets, (4) the `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` post-filter path when `offset` is negative.

Pre-existing typo `queryset.query.order_b` is one line from the changed code

On the unchanged line 105 of `BasePaginator.build_queryset`, the assignment reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` instead of `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`. This is a typo that would raise `AttributeError: 'Query' object has no attribute 'order_b'` whenever the code path is reached (DESC ordering on a queryset that already has `-%s` in its order_by and `asc=True`). The PR is touching the very same `BasePaginator.get_result` / pagination file; the typo should be fixed in this PR while the area is being modified, since the bug is reachable and would be exercised by anything that pre-applies `-datetime` and then pages forward via `cursor.is_prev=False`.

`BasePaginator.get_result` silently changes behavior for every paginator subclass

The diff modifies `BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and any other subclass) from `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` followed by `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. This is not localized to `OptimizedCursorPaginator`; it changes the contract for every existing paginator. The 'Performance optimization' comment is misleading: this is a defensive clamp, not an optimization. The change is also inconsistent - negative offsets are only clamped for forward (`is_prev=False`) cursors; backward cursors still pass negative offsets straight to `queryset[offset:stop]`, which has the same crash potential. The behavior change should be scoped to the new paginator and either documented or rejected with a `BadPaginationError`.

`enable_advanced_features` is gated to admins but provides no functional benefit

The only behavioral difference between `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and `BasePaginator` (when `enable_advanced_features=True`) is the negative-offset branch, which crashes Django (see other finding). The endpoint hard-codes `enable_advanced_features=True` whenever `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. So the entire feature shipped behind admin-only access is non-functional, while still adding ~100 lines of duplicated code, an `optimized_pagination` query-string toggle, and a new exported class. The PR should either implement what the comments describe or be reduced to a no-op flag until a real implementation exists.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset QuerySet slicing will fail at runtime, contradicting the inline comment

When `enable_advanced_features` is on and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative `start_offset`. The comment above asserts "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", but Django's docs state "Negative indexing (qs[-1]) is not supported" and the compiler translates a negative low mark directly into a SQL `OFFSET -N` clause, which is invalid SQL. The very first time an admin hits the new code path the consumer will either raise `AssertionError` from the queryset machinery or produce a database error from the generated SQL. The "advanced" path needs to be reworked to actually work (e.g. reverse ordering + a positive offset, or a count-based tail query), or removed.

false_positives.candidate:
"Performance optimization" comments about negative offsets are factually wrong

Three comments in this PR (cursors.py:26-27, paginator.py:179-181, paginator.py:874-878) claim that allowing negative cursor offsets is a "performance optimization" that enables "efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning" and "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". This is incorrect: a negative offset still requires walking to that position in the result set (in SQL terms it is still an OFFSET, just expressed as a negative number). The comments advertise a benefit that the change does not deliver, which is misleading to future readers and will mislead anyone trying to reason about pagination cost.

Defensive per-segment span-count cap silently removed from the flush side

The old `_load_segment_data` aborted and dropped a segment when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, with an explicit metric/logger. That check is gone in the new version, so the only cap on segment size is now the insert-time `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua. If the insert cap is ever bypassed (older consumer version still running, manual redis writes, or a future script change), the flusher will happily scan and ship arbitrarily large segments, with corresponding memory and downstream cost. Keep the flush-side cap (or an equivalent assertion) as a defense-in-depth bound, or add a test that exercises the case where the insert-time cap is disabled.

Hard KeyError on Kafka messages missing end_timestamp_precise

process_batch now constructs `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"])`. The new `end_timestamp_precise` field has no default, so any incoming ingest-spans message that omits it will raise from the consumer and stall that batch. Even if the current producer always sets it, an index lookup with no `.get(..., 0.0)` fallback is fragile for a producer/consumer pipeline where the schema can evolve. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (or a typed default) and let the new zset score handle missing/zero values gracefully.

Headline eviction behavior is not covered by any test

The stated purpose of this PR is "eviction during insert": add-buffer.lua now does `zpopmin` once the segment set exceeds 1000 entries, and `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` were rewritten around sorted sets (zadd with `end_timestamp_precise` as score, zscan returning `(member, score)`). None of the existing tests in tests/sentry/spans/ exercise either behavior - no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction cap and the score ordering, and no test verifies that the score passed to zadd survives through to the flusher. A regression in the score key, the cap, or the eviction order could ship undetected.

Redirect-follow loop bound cut 10x with no rationale; warning comment deleted

The Lua `for i = 0, 10000 do` bound for resolving parent redirects was reduced to `for i = 0, 1000 do`, and the comment that explicitly documented the consequence ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted in the same change. With the new bound, segment trees whose redirect chain is longer than 1000 will silently stop being joined: the loop exits while `new_set_span` is still a different key, the final `hset` then writes a wrong redirect, and subsequent spans get routed into the wrong set instead of being merged. This is a data-integrity regression that should either be reverted or come with an explicit justification for why a shallower limit is now acceptable.

Unrelated OptimizedCursorPaginator and audit-logs branch added to a spans-buffer PR

The PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and the description is just "Test 2", yet the diff also introduces an entirely new OptimizedCursorPaginator class (paginator.py:821) and a parallel branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint (organization_auditlogs.py:68-83) that switches to it whenever `?optimized_pagination=true` is supplied and the caller is a superuser or has global access. Inside that branch `enable_advanced_features=True` is hardcoded, so the only gates are the new query param and the role check. None of this is related to the stated purpose of the PR, there is no justification or doc for the new endpoint flag, the new paginator has no tests, and the audit-logs branch is not tested. This should be split into a separate PR with its own description, security review, and tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache invalidation function is never called

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but no code anywhere calls it. Because the cache TTL is 60 seconds, when a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (e.g. during a rollback), that project will continue to receive upsampled `count()` results for up to 60 seconds, producing incorrect (inflated) counts in production. The docstring acknowledges that 'allowlist changes are infrequent' but does not justify serving incorrect data after removals. The cache should be invalidated synchronously when the option changes, or the option lookup itself should not be cached.

Cache returns truthy cached_result but stores strict booleans inconsistently

`cache.get(cache_key)` returns `cached_result` which was stored as a Python `bool` (`is_eligible`), but the return path does `return cached_result and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform(...)`. If `is_eligible` was `False`, the cached value is `False` and the short-circuit returns `False`, skipping the dataset check — this means a request whose project set is not allowlisted will never even consult the dataset/transactions filter, which is fine. However, if the cache backend ever returns a non-bool truthy value (e.g. some serializers wrap booleans), the `and` chain would produce unexpected types. More importantly, the dataset/sample_weight check is intentionally re-evaluated on every cache hit even though it has no dependency on the cached value's inputs, so the caching only saves the `options.get` and the per-project allowlist scan — but the cache key itself varies by project set, so hit rate for any given key is low. This negates the claimed performance benefit.

Factory silently overwrites event sample_rate with context value

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` unconditionally assigns `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever the `error_sampling` context is present. `sample_rate` is a standard SDK-provided field on events; overwriting it from a separate `error_sampling` context (which carries a different semantic — client-side reporting rate, not SDK capture rate) can corrupt downstream consumers that read `sample_rate` for ingest sampling math. It should only set the field when the event doesn't already carry a `sample_rate`, or write to a distinct field. The two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks additionally hide all errors including programming mistakes.

Hard-coded count==10 assumes undocumented sample_weight semantics

The assertions `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` rely on `sum(sample_weight)` producing 10 when `client_sample_rate` is 0.1. That is only true if the Snuba `sample_weight` column is precomputed as `1/sample_rate` rather than equal to `sample_rate`. The factory change only sets `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)`; nothing in this PR guarantees that `sample_weight` in Snuba equals `1/sample_rate`. If `sample_weight` is NULL or equals `sample_rate`, the test will silently produce wrong counts in CI and the assertion will fail or, worse, pass against a different column. Either add an explicit comment/schema check documenting the invariant, or compute the expected value from whatever mapping actually exists.

Main public function and cache invalidation are untested

The test file covers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, but never exercises the main entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss, cache-key determinism, interaction with `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and never tests `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given the cache-related concerns above, these are exactly the paths that need direct test coverage.

Organization parameter unused in allowlist check

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` accepts `organization: Organization` but never references it. The allowlist `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is treated as a single global list of project IDs with no org scoping. If two organizations share a project ID space (e.g. in tests, or in any multi-tenant view of the option), a match in the allowlist could trigger upsampling for projects in the wrong organization. Either drop the unused parameter or actually verify each project_id belongs to `organization`.

Transform only matches literal count(), misses aliased and other count variants

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact stripped/lowercased string `count()`. It will not transform `count() as total`, `count_if(...)`, `count_unique(...)`, `count_web_vitals(...)`, etc. Any aggregation that semantically counts events but isn't literal `count()` will return non-upsampled counts in the same response, producing mixed results where some y-axes are upsampled and others are not for the same time bucket. The match should also handle aliased forms and at minimum `count_if`-style aggregates for errors, or the contract should be clearly documented.

Unrelated breaking change to user-facing error text

The error message for `topEvents <= 0` was changed from `"If topEvents needs to be at least 1"` to `"topEvents needs to be at least 1"`. This is a user-facing 400 response that has nothing to do with the PR's stated purpose (upsampled error counts). It silently changes a documented API contract, will break any tests, alerts, or downstream consumers that pattern-match the message, and should be reverted or split into a separate PR.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring matching despite claiming caution

The implementation does `'event.type:error' in query` (lowercased substring), and the docstring claims it was 'Reduced to only check for event.type:error to err on the side of caution.' Substring matching is the opposite of cautious: `NOT event.type:error` matches (the query excludes errors yet upsampling will be applied), `event.type:error_handled` matches (a non-error event type is treated as an error), and `message:"event.type:error occurred"` matches. This will cause `sum(sample_weight)` upsampled counts to be returned for queries that are explicitly about non-error events, corrupting customer-facing time series. The check should tokenize and parse the query (or at minimum require word boundaries / absence of a leading `NOT`).

setUp overwrites self.user after login_as uses it

In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` and `self.authed_user = self.user` are executed before `self.user = self.create_user()`. The login and stored `authed_user` reference the parent `APITestCase`'s user, then `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user that was never logged in. The `tags` on stored events reference this new `self.user`/`self.user2` (which are different identities than the authenticated principal), so the test fixture is internally inconsistent and any tag-based filtering or permission check against the new users will not behave as intended. Reorder setUp so users are created before login_as, or stop reassigning self.user.

upsampled_count() not registered in errors dataset

The SnQLFunction `upsampled_count` is only registered in the discover dataset's function_converter, but `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` emits `"upsampled_count() as count"` regardless of which dataset is being queried. When the errors dataset is used (which is the primary use case for error upsampling, and is the dataset that `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for unconditionally), the query will fail at the Snuba layer with an unknown-function error. The function must also be registered in the errors dataset's function converter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs zipped IDs with nodestore values that may be out of order or duplicated

`fetch_error_details` does `for event_id, data in zip(error_ids, events.values())`, relying on `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids).values()` to return entries in the same order as `node_ids`. If `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a mapping whose iteration order does not strictly match the request order (some cache backends do not guarantee this), or if `error_ids` contains duplicates and the implementation deduplicates internally, then `event_id` and `data` will be mismatched: the wrong title/timestamp/message will be associated with the wrong event id when feeding error context to the LLM. Iterate `events` by explicit node_id lookup (e.g. `[events.get(nid) for nid in node_ids]`) to make ordering explicit.
