false_positives.candidate:
Broad `except Exception` in get_environment_info silently swallows errors

`get_environment_info` wraps its entire body (including `issue.get_recommended_event()` and `recommended_event.get_environment()`) in `except Exception`, only logs at info level, and returns an empty string. If anything in the recommended-event / environment lookup regresses, this will silently drop environment info from every GitHub/GitLab suspect-PR comment with no alert. At minimum, narrow the catch to the specific exceptions that can be raised (e.g. `Group.DoesNotExist`, `Environment.DoesNotExist`) and/or log at warning/error level.

MatchedRow.max_segment_id type change lacks test for the None branch

`MatchedRow` is updated so `max_segment_id: int | None`, and `_make_recording_filenames` short-circuits when it is `None`. The corresponding test change only flips an existing fixture from `0` to `None` to exercise the early return, but does not assert that no deletion request is made when `max_segment_id` is `None` (no chunks produced, archive-only path). A regression that deletes despite `None` would not be caught by the existing test as-is.

ParameterizationRegexExperiment removed without deprecation

The `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` class is removed from `__all__`, the `ParameterizationExperiment` union type alias no longer includes it, and the option `grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent` is deleted. Any external consumer or downstream test that still references `ParameterizationRegexExperiment` will fail with `ImportError` or `TypeError`. If this class is genuinely unused, this is fine, but the public export should be removed deliberately and a deprecation cycle would be safer given `__all__` is exported.

Removal of 'browser_report_received' info log not covered by remaining tests

The previous endpoint logged `logger.info('browser_report_received', extra={'request_body': request.data})` for every accepted request. The new endpoint removes this log. The test file drops `test_logs_request_data_if_option_enabled` and the new `test_basic` does not assert any logger.info behavior. If the original intent of the endpoint was to capture raw browser reports (the PR description for the original feature indicated GCP forwarding), this log loss should be intentional and documented, or the test asserting the log should be retained.

Renaming analytics event 'replay.view_html' to 'replay.view-html' breaks downstream consumers

`trackAnalytics('replay.view_html', ...)` is renamed to `trackAnalytics('replay.view-html', ...)`. The internal type registry in `replayAnalyticsEvents.tsx` is updated to match, but any external dashboards, alerts, or saved queries that filter on the old `replay.view_html` event name will silently stop receiving data. Renaming a published analytics event key is an API contract break and should be deprecated, not renamed silently, or at minimum called out clearly in the release notes.

Visualize API silently breaks multi-y-axis support and changes stacking behavior

The `Visualize` constructor now takes a single `yAxis: string` instead of `yAxes: readonly string[]`, and `this.stack = 'all'` is now unconditional. Previously, bar charts with multiple y-axes rendered with `stack === undefined` (unstacked), and `Visualize.replace({yAxes: [...]})` could mutate the y-axis list. Any saved view, link, or component that constructs `new Visualize([...])` or `replace({yAxes: [...]})` will silently produce wrong data or fail. Additionally, callers of `Visualize.fromJSON(json)` previously received a single `Visualize`; the new signature returns `Visualize[]`. Code that did `Visualize.fromJSON(x).replace(...)` will break (`.replace` is undefined on an array). This is a breaking change to a user-facing feature and should be called out in the PR description / release notes.

noise_config added to DBQueryInjectionVulnerabilityGroupType without comment

A `noise_config = NoiseConfig(ignore_limit=5)` is added to `DBQueryInjectionVulnerabilityGroupType` without any inline comment explaining why this group type is being treated as noisy at a 5-event limit. Group-type noise configs are product decisions that affect alerting/grouping behavior and should be reviewed; at minimum a comment should explain the rationale so future maintainers don't remove it by mistake.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code comparison is case sensitive and can fail for valid hex codes

`backupCodes` is produced by `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, which is lowercase. The lookup compares `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` against the array with `indexOf` without normalising case, and `next-auth-options.ts` does the same. A user who copy‑pastes or types the code with uppercase letters (e.g. via autofill, or because the UI only displays a placeholder pattern `XXXXX-XXXXX` and the user assumes either case works) will be rejected with `IncorrectBackupCode` even though the code is correct. Normalise both sides to lowercase before comparing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition allows a single backup code to authenticate multiple concurrent logins

In the backup code branch the lookup is `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` followed by `backupCodes[index] = null` and a plain `prisma.user.update` that re‑encrypts the array. Two concurrent requests that both submit the same valid backup code can both read the same index, both set it to null, and both `update` the row. The result is two authenticated sessions for one single‑use code. The lookup/mutation needs to be wrapped in a transaction with a row-level lock (or otherwise made atomic, e.g. by storing a hash plus a per-code marker) so that the second concurrent attempt fails with `IncorrectBackupCode`. The same race exists for any caller that re-uses a code in parallel.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`backupCodesUrl` Blob is never revoked when the modal is closed

`setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` is created on setup success and only revoked when `handleSetup` is invoked again. If the user closes the dialog without going through setup a second time, the Blob URL stays alive until the page unloads, holding the plaintext backup codes in memory. Call `URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)` in a cleanup effect (and in `resetState`) so the Blob is released deterministically.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login and backup-code disable paths have no e2e coverage

The PR adds the entire backup-code feature (login flow, display, copy/download, disabling 2FA via backup code) but the e2e test only exercises the TOTP login and TOTP‑based disable. The `// TODO: add more backup code tests` comment confirms the gap. There is no test that (a) re-logs in using a generated backup code via the `Lost access` button, (b) disables 2FA with a backup code, or (c) verifies that a used backup code can no longer authenticate. These are the core acceptance criteria for the issue and must be covered before merging.

Backup-code branch bypasses password verification when `totpCode` is also present

Password verification is gated by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`, so any request that includes a non-empty `totpCode` skips password validation entirely. The backup-code branch then takes priority over the TOTP branch (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`). An attacker who has obtained a valid backup code (e.g. by shoulder-surfing the setup screen, by stealing the user's download, or via the race condition above) can simply include any non-empty string as `totpCode` together with the backup code, and password verification is skipped. Either verify the password whenever a password is set regardless of `totpCode`, or restrict the backup-code branch so it only runs when password has already been verified.

Cancel handler invokes `onCancel` before resetting local state

The cancel button calls `onCancel()` and then `resetState()`. The parent is likely to hide the modal (or unmount the page) in response to `onCancel`, which can race with the second `resetState()` call and leave the component in a partially reset condition. Reverse the order: `resetState()` then `onCancel()`. The same pattern issue applies to the backup-codes close button at lines 266-269 (`onEnable()` before `resetState()`).

No protection against malformed/corrupted `backupCodes` ciphertext

The handler does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` with no try/catch. If the stored ciphertext is corrupted, the JSON is invalid, or the encryption key was rotated without re-encrypting old values, the exception bubbles up as a 500 with no actionable error. The login handler in `next-auth-options.ts` has the same shape. Wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch and return `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` (or a new dedicated error) so the UI can show a sensible message and so the failure mode is not a generic 500.

Password field in disable modal is rendered without a label

The `PasswordField` is given `labelProps={{ className: "block text-sm font-medium text-default" }}` but no `label` prop, so `PasswordField` falls back to no label text and the styling from `labelProps` has nothing to attach to. Users opening the "Disable 2FA" dialog see an unlabeled text field and may not understand they must re-enter their account password. Pass `label={t("password")}` (matching what `EnableTwoFactorModal` does) so the dialog is self-explanatory.

`<Label>` is not associated with the input via `htmlFor`

The `Label` element renders the `t("backup_code")` string but has no `htmlFor` attribute, while the `TextField` declares `id="backup-code"`. Screen readers will not announce them as related and clicking the label text will not focus the input. Add `htmlFor="backup-code"` to the `Label`.

`TextField` length attributes ignore the dash in the middle

`minLength={10}` / `maxLength={11}` describe the raw character count, but the field is also visually presented as `XXXXX-XXXXX` and the server strips dashes before comparing (`replaceAll("-", "")`). Users may legitimately type 11 characters including the dash and be exactly at the limit, which is fine, but the placeholder and helper text never explain that the dash is optional. Either accept input with or without the dash consistently (currently accepted on the server but the length limits are tight against the user's expectation) or document/format the input so the count is obvious. Also, `required` plus `minLength={10}` makes the HTML5 validity message "Please lengthen this text to 10 characters or more (you are currently using X characters)" which is technically wrong for the dashed form (11 with dash, 10 without). Consider deriving the limits from the formatted length (11) and normalising before validation.

`formatBackupCode` is referenced before its declaration

`handleSetup` (line 77) references `formatBackupCode` inside its body, but `formatBackupCode` is declared with `const` at line 163, below the function definition. It works at runtime because `handleSetup` only runs after the component has rendered, but the order is confusing and tools that analyse temporal dead zones / eslint `no-use-before-define` will complain. Move the `formatBackupCode` definition above `handleSetup`.

`resetState` leaves backup codes, secret, QR data URI and the object URL in state

`resetState` only clears `password`, `errorMessage` and `step`. It does not clear `backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl`, `dataUri` or `secret`. The `cancel` button at lines 224-230 calls `resetState()` then closes the modal, but because the dialog is controlled (state persists while `open` toggles), a subsequent re-open of the modal can briefly render the previous user's QR/secret/backup codes while the new password-confirm step is shown, or the `backupCodesUrl` Blob URL keeps pointing at stale data. Reset all of the 2FA-related state in `resetState` and revoke `backupCodesUrl` with `URL.revokeObjectURL` before clearing it.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TypeError crash when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet

After the destinationCalendar is converted to an array, this fallback uses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without an optional chain. When `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null` or `[]` (which is a common case handled by every caller of this function, e.g. when the user selected Google Meet as the location but has no Google Calendar configured on Cal, which previously was a soft "fallback to Cal Video" path), `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = ... ?? []` yields `undefined`, and the next expression `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')`. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"` and would safely fall back to Cal Video; the new code crashes before the fallback can occur. This regression breaks the entire Meet-location code path for any booking without a Google destination calendar.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Broken fallback for updateEvent when externalCalendarId is missing

In `updateEvent`, the fallback for when `externalCalendarId` is not provided is now `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When `externalCalendarId` is `null`/undefined (which happens for legacy bookings stored before this PR that do not have `BookingReference.externalCalendarId` populated), the predicate compares `cal.externalId === undefined` and never matches, so the result is `undefined`. The previous code `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` correctly fell back to the first destination calendar's externalId. With this change, update calls that previously succeeded now hit Google with `calendarId: undefined` and fail. The intent appears to be "pick the destination calendar for this credential", so the find should compare against `credentialId` (or the caller should pass it through), not against the already-undefined `externalCalendarId`. The same broken pattern is present in `deleteEvent` (see next finding).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Broken fallback for deleteEvent when externalCalendarId is missing

The deleteEvent fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` exhibits the same bug as updateEvent: when `externalCalendarId` is undefined/null, the predicate cannot match, so `calendarId` ends up `undefined` and Google receives a delete call without a `calendarId` (only the `defaultCalendarId = "primary"` ternary saves it when `calendarId` is falsy). For legacy bookings that don't store an externalCalendarId on the reference, this silently routes deletions to "primary" instead of the correct destination calendar. The fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` before this PR, and the rewrite removes that legitimate fallback without providing a working one.

Team destination calendars not added when no event-type or organizer calendar exists

The event's `destinationCalendar` is set by the chain to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` is set. The subsequent line `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` uses optional chaining and silently no-ops on `null`. As a result, in the very scenario the PR is meant to fix — a COLLECTIVE event where the event-type has no destination calendar and the organizer (first host) has no destination calendar but other team members do — the team members' `destinationCalendar` values are never attached to `evt.destinationCalendar`, and `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` falls back to "the first connected calendar" instead of creating the event in each host's calendar. The push should be a normal assignment that initialises the array if needed, e.g. `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`. Also note that if `eventType.destinationCalendar` is set, pushing team members onto the same array may create duplicate references for the same DestinationCalendar record.

Team members may be excluded when first user in array is not the organizer

The new `teamDestinationCalendars` is built from `users.slice(1)`, i.e. it always excludes whichever user happens to be at index 0 in the `users` array. For dynamic events `users` is populated from `prisma.user.findMany({ where: { username: { in: dynamicUserList } } })` with no `orderBy`, so the index-0 user may not be the organizer. If the actual organizer happens to be at index 0 they are correctly excluded (their calendar is taken from `organizerUser.destinationCalendar`), but if they are not, their `destinationCalendar` is lost from `teamDestinationCalendars` because `.slice(1)` indiscriminately cuts the first element. The exclusion should be keyed on whether the user is the organizer (e.g. by id/username), not on array index.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutates parsed result by setting refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token"

If the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the helper does `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. The string "refresh_token" is not a valid OAuth refresh token; any caller that persists this object (directly or via spread) will end up storing a placeholder value, causing the next refresh attempt to fail with invalid_grant. This affects the standard schemas (e.g. `refreshTokenResponseSchema`, `googleCredentialSchema`) that mark `refresh_token` optional. The mutation also has no TypeScript escape hatch – the helper writes a property that may not exist on the inferred type.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema does not declare an index signature, validation will always fail

The schema uses `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`, but those are computed property names that evaluate to the strings "ZodString" and "ZodOptional" at runtime, not TypeScript index signatures. As a result the parsed object must contain a literal `ZodString: number` property in addition to `access_token`, which OAuth token responses never have. Whenever the credential-sync flow is active, `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` returns `{success: false}` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", so every credential refresh attempted via the sync endpoint will fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Returns SafeParseResult instead of parsed data; Google Calendar persists the wrapper

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full `safeParse` result object (`{success: true, data: ...}`), but `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` consumes it as if it were the parsed key: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. This causes the database row to be overwritten with `{success: true, data: {…token fields…}}` rather than the token fields themselves. On the next request `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will fail and the credential becomes effectively unusable.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync endpoint returns a fetch Response while callers expect axios / typed token objects

When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response`. Several callers assume their original axios / jsforce shape:
- `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts`: treats the return value as `HubspotToken` and reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate` and `.expiresIn` (undefined on a Response) and writes back `expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` → NaN persisted as the expiry.
- `zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts` and `zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts`: read `tokenInfo.data.error`, `tokenInfo.data.expiryDate`, etc. on what is now a `Response` object – `undefined.error` throws.
- `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`: reads `res?.data.access_token` – undefined, throwing on `.access_token`.
The sync path therefore crashes the refresh for several integrations instead of delegating to the user's endpoint.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync endpoint returns a fetch Response while callers expect axios / typed token objects

When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response`. Several callers assume their original axios / jsforce shape:
- `hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts`: treats the return value as `HubspotToken` and reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate` and `.expiresIn` (undefined on a Response) and writes back `expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` → NaN persisted as the expiry.
- `zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts` and `zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts`: read `tokenInfo.data.error`, `tokenInfo.data.expiryDate`, etc. on what is now a `Response` object – `undefined.error` throws.
- `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`: reads `res?.data.access_token` – undefined, throwing on `.access_token`.
The sync path therefore crashes the refresh for several integrations instead of delegating to the user's endpoint.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zoho-bigin passes credential.id where user.id is expected

`refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)` calls `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)`. `refreshOAuthTokens` then POSTs `calcomUserId=${credentialId}` (the `Credential.id`, not `User.id`) to the self-hoster's sync endpoint, so the parent cannot resolve the user. Every other caller (Hubspot, Office365 video, Lark, Webex, Zoom, ZohoCRM) correctly forwards `credential.userId`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Body validation throws and bubbles as 500 instead of returning 400

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a Zod error when the body is malformed. Next.js converts that into a generic 500, while the rest of the handler consistently returns structured 400/403/404 JSON. Callers (the self-hoster's parent app) will not be able to distinguish malformed payloads from server errors.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED combines two unrelated flags and yields a non-boolean

`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. With an empty string for either env var this evaluates to the empty string (or the other env var), not `false`, and downstream code uses it as a truthy check (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`) – empty string is falsy so it happens to work, but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` later does `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT)`, so the semantics depend on whether the env var is the literal `"false"`/`"0"` or empty. Coerce to a boolean explicitly and either include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` in the gate or document the partial activation mode.

Header lookup uses env var verbatim, but Node lowercases request headers

`req.headers` in Node stores header names in lowercase. The handler looks up `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`. If an operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` to any mixed/upper-case value, the lookup is `undefined` and every request is rejected with 403, even when the secret itself is correct. The constant should be lowercased before use, or compared against `req.headers[name.toLowerCase()]`.

Salesforce refresh bypasses refreshOAuthTokens entirely

`getClient` issues the refresh POST directly to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and then runs it through `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, but it never routes through `refreshOAuthTokens`. The result is that for self-hosters that turn on `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, Salesforce refresh tokens continue to be exchanged against Salesforce directly instead of being fetched from the configured parent service – inconsistent with every other calendar/video integration modified here, and undermining the purpose of the feature for Salesforce users.

Unnecessary database round-trip before appStoreMetadata lookup

The handler queries `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug: reqBody.appSlug } })` and then immediately re-resolves the same slug against the in-memory `appStoreMetadata` map. The DB call adds latency to a public webhook and is redundant: validating against `appStoreMetadata` directly (and 404ing if absent) gives the same behaviour without hitting Postgres.

Webhook allows writing OAuth tokens for any user with no per-user authorization

The endpoint authenticates the caller only via the shared `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` header; the request body supplies `userId` directly. There is no binding between caller identity and the target user (no signature of the userId, no per-user secret, no replay protection/nonce, no rate limit). Anyone in possession of the secret can therefore upsert OAuth credentials for any userId, including admin accounts, and effectively impersonate them. Because the secret is also required to be 32 bytes for AES-256, a leak is catastrophic for the instance.

Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time

`req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` performs a non-constant-time string comparison, exposing the webhook secret to timing attacks. Anyone able to observe response latencies could recover the secret character by character. Because this single shared secret authorizes writes of OAuth credentials for arbitrary `userId` values (see below), a leaked secret enables full impersonation of any user via injected tokens. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over equal-length buffers.

findFirst + create/update upsert is racy

The handler does a `findFirst` followed by separate `update`/`create` calls rather than a single `upsert`/transaction. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same `(userId, appSlug)` can both observe `appCredential === null` and both insert, leaving duplicate `Credential` rows for the same user/app and breaking the assumption made elsewhere in the codebase (larkcalendar, office365video, webex, zoom callbacks) that there is at most one credential per `(type, appId, userId)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist check is case-sensitive

`BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` is lowercased on parse, but the input `guest` is not lowercased before `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. Submitting `BLOCKED@example.com` against a blacklist entry `blocked@example.com` will bypass the block. The guest value must be lowercased before being checked against the blacklist.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin permission requires user to be both admin AND owner

The permission check `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))` requires the caller to be BOTH a team admin and a team owner. Since `isTeamAdmin` typically already returns true for owners, the AND collapses the check to "owner only" — team admins lose the ability to add guests. The operator should be `||` (or the `isTeamAdmin` call should be dropped, as it already covers owners). With the current code, only team owners can use the new feature even though the UI claims any admin/owner can.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails sends AttendeeScheduledEmail to new guests using raw input emails

The handler passes the raw `guests` input (which may contain case variants or duplicates) as `newGuests`, and `sendAddGuestsEmails` does `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` to decide between `AttendeeScheduledEmail` and `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. Because the match is case-sensitive and the input was not deduplicated/normalized, the wrong email template is sent in the obvious cases (e.g. `Alice@x.com` vs `alice@x.com`) and a duplicate email is sent if the same address was submitted twice with different casing. The list of "new" guests should be built from the normalized `uniqueGuests` and lowercased before comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Server-side schema does not enforce uniqueness, allowing duplicate rows

`ZAddGuestsInputSchema` only validates email format; uniqueness is only enforced in the client `AddGuestsDialog`. A malicious or buggy client can POST `["a@x.com", "a@x.com"]` and the handler will create two `Attendee` rows for the same address. The server schema should `.refine` for uniqueness (ideally after lowercasing) and the handler's `uniqueGuests` filter should also be the source of truth for the DB write — currently `prisma.booking.update(... createMany: data: guestsFullDetails)` uses `uniqueGuests`, but the email pass later (`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`) uses the raw `guests` input, which can still mis-trigger the duplicate `AttendeeScheduledEmail` branch in `email-manager.ts`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dialog sends empty email rows through validation and fails with a misleading message

`MultiEmail` initializes `value` with `[""]` and the "Add Another" button pushes another `""`. The dialog validates the raw `multiEmailValue` array, so leaving any field blank (e.g. `["a@x.com", "", "b@x.com"]`) or submitting immediately on open fails `z.array(z.string().email())` and shows "Emails must be unique and valid", which does not describe the actual problem (blank fields). The handler should `.transform`/filter out empty strings (and lowercase + trim) before parsing, and surface a more specific message — otherwise users will repeatedly hit this confusing error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
AddGuestsDialog is always mounted for every booking row

The `<AddGuestsDialog>` is rendered unconditionally for every `BookingListItem` (and the BookingListItem table can render hundreds of rows). The dialog content is always in the DOM, registering tRPC mutation hooks for every row. The dialog should only be mounted when `isOpenAddGuestsDialog` is true (the same pattern other dialogs in this file already use), to avoid hundreds of stale mutation handles and extra DOM nodes on the bookings list page.

Cancelled/rejected/past bookings can have guests added

After loading the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status`. A caller can add guests to a CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-past booking, which will create new attendees, push them to the connected calendar, and send "guests added" emails about an event that is no longer happening. The handler must reject when the booking is not in an `ACCEPTED` (or `PENDING`) state, and ideally also when `booking.endTime < now()`.

Deduplication is case-sensitive, allowing near-duplicate attendees

Both the existing-attendee check (`guest === attendee.email`) and the email format assumed by the rest of the app treat emails as case-sensitive, but emails are case-insensitive by RFC. A caller can submit `Alice@Example.com` while an existing attendee is `alice@example.com` and the new one will be added as a separate row, creating duplicate attendees in `Booking.attendees` and duplicate calendar invites. All comparisons should lowercase both sides before comparing, and the schema should normalize input.

Email send failure is silently swallowed

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` call is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }`. The DB has already been mutated and the calendar has already been updated, so the API returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` and the UI shows the success toast even when no emails went out. Either surface the error (so the UI can retry/notify) or skip the DB write until emails have been queued.

Error toast displays raw TRPC code instead of a useful translation key

On error the toast uses `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`. For zod-input failures `err.message` is a generic zod string (e.g. the literal string `"BAD_REQUEST"` is not a translation key), so users see `BAD_REQUEST: BAD_REQUEST` or a missing-translation key. The handler should throw `TRPCError`s with translation-key messages (like the existing `emails_must_be_unique_valid`/`you_do_not_have_permission`), and the client should prefer `t(err.message)` only when the key exists, falling back to `unable_to_add_guests` otherwise.

No transactional boundary between DB write and calendar/email side effects

`prisma.booking.update` runs first, then `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`, then `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`. None of this is in a transaction. If the calendar call or email send throws, the DB is left with attendees added but the connected calendar/videocall still missing them, and the user sees a 500 even though the mutation was half-applied. The whole flow should be wrapped (DB update + calendar update + email send) so a failure leaves no partial state, or the email/calendar steps should run before the DB write with a compensating delete on failure.

No upper bound on guests array length

The schema accepts an unbounded array of emails and the handler will happily create that many attendees, update the calendar, and fan out N emails. A malicious caller can submit thousands of addresses to cause resource exhaustion and email bombing. Add `z.array(...).min(1).max(N)` (with N chosen to match the event type's `seatsPerTimeSlot` / max attendees setting) and consider reusing `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` plus rate limiting.

Team bookings crash with Prisma RecordNotFound

For team/round-robin bookings, `booking.userId` is often null. The handler does `where: { id: booking.userId || 0 }` when looking up the organizer, so it issues `findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: 0 } })`, which throws an unwrapped `Prisma.RecordNotFound` error and returns a 500 to the client instead of a meaningful error. The lookup needs to handle `booking.userId == null` explicitly (e.g. resolve the organizer from `eventType.team` or return a clean `NOT_FOUND`/`BAD_REQUEST`).

userPrimaryEmail is always undefined, silently falling back to organizer.email

The Prisma `booking` query does not select `userPrimaryEmail`, so `booking?.userPrimaryEmail ?? organizer.email` always resolves to `organizer.email`. This is unlikely to be a security issue (the booking's organizer email is also pulled from the same user record), but the misleading fallback hides the intent. If the original design is to honor the organizer's primary email for calendar invites, the field needs to be added to the `select`/`include`; otherwise the dead branch should be removed.

{...props} spread after named props allows caller to silently override intended fields

`{...props}` is spread after `title`, `headerType`, `subject`, and `callToAction`, so if any caller (including `organizer-add-guests-email.ts` if extended) ever passes one of those keys, the intended value is silently overridden. deleteMany cleanup is not scoped to SMS method

If the data ever drifts so the org itself is excluded from `teamIds` (or if the query is later changed to fetch only sub-team memberships to optimize), those users' non-team bookings will silently disappear from org-scope insights. The pre-existing object-based version had the same shape, so this is not a regression, but the SQL rewrite is a good opportunity to make the intent explicit (and to add an integration test for an org member without any sub-team membership).

In the new reschedule block, the call is `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true)` — passing `immediateDelete: true` causes an immediate SendGrid POST to /v3/user/scheduled_sends with status:'cancel' for every workflow reminder of the previous booking. Under any burst of simultaneous reschedules the limit will be reached and old reminders will be delivered (the exact bug being fixed). Pass `false` (or omit) to be consistent with the cancel path.

In the new block (lines 53-77) the loop calls `await client.request(...)` for every reminder and only after success builds a `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` and pushes it into `workflowRemindersToDelete`. When `client.request` throws (e.g. SendGrid's documented limit on pending cancellations is reached, batch_id not found, or transient API error), the throw escapes the for-loop into the outer try/catch which only logs and returns. Consequences: (1) every reminder after the first failure is silently skipped in this run; (2) the deletes already pushed for the successful iterations are never executed because `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is skipped after the throw — they become dangling promises that may or may not resolve in the background with no observability. For EMAIL reminders, a failure to set `cancelled: true` in the DB means the CRON-driven SendGrid cancellation never happens and the attendee receives the old reminder email. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `await Promise.all(reminders.map(async r => ...))`, so the DB row is reliably marked (and the Twilio call observed) before the mutation responds.

Working-hours check sets end equal to start, ignoring event length

In the newly added working-hours branch of `checkIfIsAvailable`, the local `end` variable is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`, which is identical to `start`. The intent (from the variable names and the surrounding comment `slot is outside of working hours`) was clearly to compare the slot's end time against `workingHour.endTime`. false_negatives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override day comparison mixes local-mode and UTC-mode dayjs objects

The comparison `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is incorrect: `dayjs(date.start).add(...)` returns a Dayjs in the default (system local) timezone, so its `.format("YYYY MM DD")` is rendered in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime = time.utc()` is explicitly in UTC mode and formats in UTC. As a result the comparison only matches when the server happens to run in UTC (or in the same offset as the override), and silently fails in any other deployment timezone, causing date overrides to be missed entirely or applied on the wrong day. Both sides must use `.tz(organizerTimeZone)` (e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD")`), or both must be forced to UTC with `.utc()`.

Date-override offset formula does not compute wall-clock time in invitee tz

The new block computes `const offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset;` and then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() / .minute()` to derive `startTime`/`endTime`. This does not produce the minute-of-day in the invitee's timezone. Worked example: override at 14:00 IST is stored as `override.start = 1970-01-01T08:30:00.000Z`. With invitee in Asia/Dhaka (+06:00) the code gives `offset = 30`, then `dayjs(08:30Z).utc().add(30m).hour() = 9`, so `startTime = 540` (09:00), i.e. slots appear at 09:00 Asia/Dhaka = 03:00 UTC. The correct value is `14:30 Asia/Dhaka = 08:30 UTC`, which would come from `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour()*60 + .minute()`. As a result, for the production data shape (UTC moment encoding the organizer's wall clock) the PR silently shifts all date-override slots by the full timezone offset between organizer and invitee (e.g. 5h30m for IST→UTC, 5h for IST→EST).

Date-override test uses literal-UTC times instead of organizer wall-clock times

The `IstWorkHoursWithDateOverride` fixture stores the override as `{ startTime: "1970-01-01T14:00:00.000Z", endTime: "1970-01-01T18:00:00.000Z" }` and a schedule timeZone of `+05:30`, but the test's own name comment says the override is "2PM to 6PM IST". In production a Cal.com date override is the UTC moment that represents the organizer's local wall clock, so a 14:00 IST override is stored as `1970-01-01T08:30:00.000Z`. The fixture instead stores the literal UTC time 14:00, which happens to make the buggy `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` formula in `packages/lib/slots.ts` produce the right UTC slots by accident (both IST and Asia/Dhaka invitees see `08:30Z`). With the production shape the PR's formula would emit slots shifted by the full organizer↔invitee offset and the tests would fail, so this gap is hiding the high-severity timezone bug above.

Webhook signature in test_github_user_mismatch won't match the modified payload

The test mutates webhook_event["installation"]["id"] and webhook_event["sender"]["login"] and then re-serializes with json.dumps(webhook_event), but it sends the hard-coded signature sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486. That signature was computed over the original bytes of INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE; modifying any field changes the HMAC input, so the GitHub webhook endpoint will reject the request with a non-2xx response. The test will fail at `assert resp.status_code == 204`, the Integration record is never created, and the subsequent user-mismatch branch in GitHubInstallation is therefore never exercised. The new security check is added without a working test that proves it actually rejects a mismatched sender.

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch(), safe_urlread and parse_qsl are wrapped in `try/except Exception` so any decode/parse failure yields an empty payload and triggers the error page. The preceding `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` call is NOT inside that try block, so any network error, DNS failure, timeout, or non-2xx from safe_urlopen propagates out of dispatch and crashes the request as a 500 instead of returning the error page. The same problem applies to the immediately following `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` call at line 434, which is also outside the try block. Both should be wrapped so all token-exchange failures produce the same user-visible error response.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 branch

The test name and the responses.replace(...status=404) suggest it is verifying the path where get_installation_info returns 404 (which should produce "The GitHub installation could not be found."). In the new flow, the first GET (with only installation_id) hits OAuthLoginView, which binds the id and redirects to GitHub OAuth without ever calling get_installation_info. The second GET uses state='ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' which cannot equal pipeline.signature, so the response is the generic state-mismatch error page ("Invalid installation request.") rather than the installation-not-found error. The build_integration 404 branch is therefore no longer covered by any test, and the renamed assertion no longer checks what the test name implies.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes default of 1 contradicts PR goal

The CLI option defaults to 1 and the help text reads 'Defaults to 1'. With `flusher_processes=1` the flusher remains a single process handling all assigned shards, exactly matching the prior behavior and contradicting the PR description 'make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard'. The factory falls back to `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing 0 would auto-scale but the CLI default of 1 silently disables the new behavior. The default should be 0 (auto), or the help text/help should clearly indicate operators must opt in to get the multi-process behavior described.

Dead method _create_process_for_shard defined but never called

The new code defines `def _create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` with logic that looks up which process owns a shard and restarts that process. It is never invoked from anywhere in the module (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly via `_ensure_processes_alive`). It is misleading dead code that should be removed or actually wired into per-shard restart paths.

Inner join loop ignores remaining_time after first wait

Inside `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time = deadline - time.time()` once before the `while process.is_alive()` loop, but never recomputes `deadline` inside that inner loop. After each `time.sleep(0.1)` the comparison `deadline > time.time()` is still correct (it uses absolute deadline), so the loop does terminate, but the initial `remaining_time` check is dead — it is computed and then never consulted again. Harmless but confusing; either remove the pre-check or actually use it to cap the total per-process wait.

Memory backpressure check likely over-aggregates Redis global memory

In the old single-buffer code, `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` returned one set of Redis memory stats. The new code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` and sums `used`/`available` across all of them. Because every SpansBuffer in `self.buffers` queries the same underlying Redis cluster, each call returns the same global `used`/`available` values; summing N copies multiplies the apparent memory by N. With the new default of N flushers (one per shard), the threshold would trip at roughly `max_memory_percentage / N` of real usage, causing the consumer to hard-pause way before Redis is actually full. Either aggregate once (deduplicating per Redis cluster) or change `get_memory_info` to report per-shard stats before summing.

Per-process backpressure raises on any one process, halting the consumer

The old code had a single `backpressure_since` for the lone flusher process; raising MessageRejected on that flag paused the consumer for the whole pipeline. The new code raises MessageRejected if *any* one of the per-process backpressure flags is over threshold. With the new shard-per-process layout a single hot shard can now trip backpressure and stop ingestion entirely, even when the other shards have plenty of headroom. The original code also fetched the `backpressure-seconds` option only when needed; the new code fetches it on every submit (small perf regression). Consider only signalling backpressure when *all* processes are stuck, or aggregating by Redis instance.

Thread flusher not joined on shutdown when produce_to_pipe is set

In `join()`, the loop waits for `process.is_alive()` to become False and then only calls `process.terminate()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. For the test path (`produce_to_pipe is not None`), the workers are `threading.Thread` daemons, so they have no `terminate()`. The code only signals them via `stopped.value`, but the main loop may exit before the thread observes the flag (especially with the monkeypatched `time.sleep`). Daemon threads will be killed when the interpreter exits, but in-process this can leak work in-flight in Redis (e.g., `done_flush_segments` not called), leaving dangling 'flushing' segment keys. Consider an explicit thread shutdown with a small bounded wait, or document the test-only restriction.

max_processes=0 falls through to len(assigned_shards) via `or`

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy, so callers that explicitly pass 0 (a common sentinel meaning 'auto/unbounded') get silently coerced to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. While 0 is not currently exposed via the CLI default (which is 1), this is a footgun for any future caller (and for the planned 'auto' default). It also makes the check indistinguishable from `None`. Use an explicit `if max_processes is None` check.

test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify shared-process flushing works

The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that `sum(len(shards) for shards in ... ) == 4`. It does not actually send any spans through `submit()`, so the multi-process/sharing code path (round-robin shard distribution, per-shard SpansBuffer instances, per-process backpressure/health values, per-shard metric tags) is never exercised. Add a case that submits spans into shards handled by each of the two threads and asserts each produced its expected message with the correct `shard` tag.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error handling test has inverted assertion

In `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, the docstring says 'Test that errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages', but the assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` expects the opposite: that no commits happen. The `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally` block, so offsets are always marked complete regardless of whether `result_processor` raised. The `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` would then return offset 101 (the highest contiguous completed), and the wrapped `commit_offsets` would commit `{partition: 102}` to Kafka via `track_commits`. The assertion would fail on a correct implementation. The test should instead assert `test_partition in committed_offsets` (or similar) to verify that errors don't block commits.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Commit/mark_committed window can re-commit same offsets

In `_commit_loop`, `self.commit_function(committable)` is called before `mark_committed` updates `last_committed`. If a later step in the same iteration raises (or the commit is slow and another `_commit_loop` tick observes the same state on the next second), `get_committable_offsets` can return the same offset set again and `commit_function` will be called twice with the same data. Kafka offset commits are idempotent so this is not a correctness bug, but the lack of atomicity between commit and state update means a duplicate commit is possible; holding a lock across both calls, or marking committed before invoking the commit function with a rollback on failure, would be cleaner.

Kafka integration test reaches into arroyo internals

`test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` calls `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` to drive the `StreamProcessor`. Both methods are underscore-prefixed private APIs of the `arroyo` library and are not part of any documented contract; future arroyo releases can rename/remove them without warning and silently break this test. The test should either use the public `run()`/`shutdown()` API or be marked as expected to fail on arroyo upgrades.

OffsetTracker lock initialization relies on CPython dict atomicity

`_get_partition_lock` uses a check-then-set pattern (`self.partition_locks.get(partition)` followed by `self.partition_locks.setdefault(...)`). While `dict.setdefault` is atomic under CPython's GIL, this is not guaranteed by the language and could create duplicate `Lock` instances for the same partition on alternative Python implementations (PyPy, Jython, etc.), causing concurrent `add_offset`/`complete_offset` calls on the same partition to operate on different locks and corrupt the `all_offsets`/`outstanding` sets. A single initialization lock or `defaultdict(threading.Lock)` would be safer and clearer.

Per-item metrics gauge in worker hot loop

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', self.work_queue.qsize(), tags={'identifier': self.identifier})` for every processed work item. For a high-throughput uptime results consumer, this emits one metrics sample per processed message, flooding the metrics pipeline. Queue depth should be reported periodically (e.g., from `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()`, which already emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.total_queued`), not per-item.

ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown leaks multiprocessing pool

`shutdown()` releases `parallel_executor` and (newly added) `queue_pool`, but never calls `self.multiprocessing_pool.shutdown()`. When mode is `parallel`, the `MultiprocessingPool` (with worker processes spawned from `multiprocessing.cpu_count()`) is left running until process exit. This is a pre-existing bug, but the PR adds a sibling `queue_pool` cleanup and is the natural place to fix it.

hash()-based group assignment is not stable across restarts

`get_queue_for_group` uses the built-in `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python randomizes string hashes per process (`PYTHONHASHSEED`), meaning the same `subscription_id` may map to a different queue index after a consumer restart. Within a single process order is preserved per queue, and Kafka offset commits ensure reprocessing starts from the right offset, so the risk of out-of-order processing is low. Flagging because `hash()` for routing is a common source of subtle ordering bugs and `hashlib` or a stable scheme (e.g., `zlib.crc32`) would be safer; reviewers should confirm this is acceptable.

worker.shutdown flag is redundant with queue.shutdown

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. The worker loop checks `self.shutdown` only at the top, but is blocked in `work_queue.get()`, so the flag has no effect until the queue is drained. After `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, `get()` raises `queue.ShutDown` once the queue is empty, so the flag is dead. Removing it (or documenting why both are needed) would make the intent clearer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' uses a scope value of false but its comment claims it allows access

The new subtest primes permCache with map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': false} and the inline comment says this 'allow[s] access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. A scope map entry with value false does not represent a granted scope — the map is effectively empty for the requested resource, so it does not actually demonstrate the intended precedence (denial cache over an allowed scope). To demonstrate that the denial cache takes precedence over a granted scope, the entry should be set to true (map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': true}); otherwise the test would pass even if the permCache lookup was silently dropped from the Check path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache entries are never invalidated, so previously-denied resources stay denied for up to 30s after a permission grant

After a Check returns Allowed=false, the code calls s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true). Nothing in this PR (or anywhere else visible in the diff) ever calls Delete on permDenialCache, so entries only expire via the 30-second TTL. Once a (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple has been denied, the user will keep receiving Allowed=false on that exact tuple for up to 30 seconds — even after a permission grant (role assignment, dashboard share, etc.) makes them eligible. This is a regression relative to the pre-PR flow, where a re-check after a grant would consult the DB and return the updated permission; the new denial cache short-circuits that re-check. As a consequence, the same user with the same role can see inconsistent behavior: a brand-new dashboard they have never asked about returns Allowed=true (no prior denial entry), while a dashboard they queried once before the grant returns Allowed=false until the entry expires. The denial cache should be invalidated (e.g., on role/permission changes or dashboard creation/sharing) so grants take effect promptly.

Denial cache key uses raw userUID while permission cache uses the resolved UID

The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw identifier parsed from the request subject by validateSubject. The permission cache key in getCachedIdentityPermissions is built from userIdentifiers.UID, the value returned by GetUserIdentifiers. GetUserIdentifiers treats a purely-numeric userUID as a user ID and resolves it to the user's canonical UID (typically a non-numeric string). For the same user, denial cache entries therefore live under one identifier and permission cache entries under another, so the two caches never share state. Concretely, if a user is identified by numeric ID '123' the denial cache is keyed by '123', while the permission cache is keyed by the resolved UID (e.g., 'abc456'); a denial cached under '123' will never block a request that arrives with subject 'user:abc456' (and vice versa). The denial cache key should be built from the same resolved UID that the permission cache uses.

No regression test for a stale denial cache entry after a permission grant

TestService_CacheCheck covers a denial cache hit that has just been written (subtest 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry'), but it does not cover the regression scenario where a denial cache entry sits for the full 30-second window while the underlying permission is granted (e.g., via role assignment or dashboard share). Given that permDenialCache has no invalidation path anywhere in the change, a test should pin down what happens when a previously-denied Check is re-run after the DB now grants the permission; with the current code the response is still Allowed=false for up to 30 seconds, and there is no test that would catch the resulting regression.

permissionCacheUsage metric conflates denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits

When the denial cache hits, Check increments permissionCacheUsage with label value 'true'. The same metric and label are used later for genuine permission-cache hits (line 132). The 'true' label therefore no longer means 'permission cache hit' — it means 'either permission cache or denial cache hit'. Existing dashboards/alerts built on this metric will silently change meaning after this PR. The denial cache hit should be recorded under a distinct metric name or a distinct label (e.g., cache='denial' vs cache='permission').
