true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission stores resource UUIDs instead of group IDs

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() the code iterates resources of type "Groups" and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the granted set. Resource IDs are UUIDs and are NOT real group IDs. Because V2 builds all-groups authorization on a single schema-typed resource rather than per-group resources, `findByName(server, groupResource.getId())` always returns null and execution falls back to `getResourceTypeResource(...)`. Any scenario where `hasPermission` succeeds (e.g. an admin granted VIEW_MEMBERS on the all-groups resource directly) results in the all-groups resource's UUID being added. Downstream consumers (UsersResource.getUsersCount, BruteForceUsersResource/UsersResource.searchForUser, which set `UserModel.GROUPS` to this set and pass it to `session.users().getUsersCount(..., groupIds)`/`searchForUserStream(..., GROUPS=...)`) treat these strings as group IDs. As a result, for an admin who only has VIEW_MEMBERS on all-groups, user search returns zero users and the count endpoint reports zero even though the admin should see users of all groups. V1's equivalent uses `resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())`; V2 needs to either return group IDs (resource names) or adopt a sentinel "all groups" semantics understood by callers, plus the search/count code must be consistent with the chosen semantics. This is not covered by the existing tests, which only grant view-members on specific groups.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug in `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission`: using `groupResource.getId()` (resource UUID) instead of the actual group ID (resource name). Both point out how this breaks `hasPermission` (falling back to the all-groups type resource because `findByName` fails) and causes downstream consumers (`UserModel.GROUPS`, `getUsersCount`) to fail because they expect actual group IDs.

false_positives.candidate:
NullPointerException risk in hasPermission when getResourceTypeResource returns null

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission, after `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` the code immediately calls `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()`. However, AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource returns null when `supportsAuthorizationSchema(session, resourceServer)` is false (e.g. the admin permissions client lookup fails or the schema resource has not yet been initialized at very early lifecycle stages). Calling `policyStore.findByResource(server, null)` will pass null into the policy store, which throws NullPointerException. Add a null check on the result of `getResourceTypeResource` before the findByResource call and return false if null. The same pattern exists in UserPermissionsV2.java at line 111.

Same null-deref risk as in GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission

The UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission method assigns the result of `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` to `resource` and then unconditionally passes it to `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()`. If `getResourceTypeResource` returns null (it can, per AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false), this throws NPE. Add a null check.

getResourceName ignores GROUPS resource type

getResourceName only contains a branch for `USERS.getType().equals(resourceType)`. With GROUPS now a first-class resource type in SCHEMA, policies for groups fall through to `return resource.getDisplayName();`. For specific group resources the `getName()` is the group's ID (per `resolveGroup`) and the display name is typically unset, so the admin UI and policy listings will show an empty string or the group id rather than the group's actual name. Add a parallel branch similar to the users branch that resolves the GroupModel by `resource.getName()` and returns `group.getName()` (and for the "all-groups" schema resource return a label such as "All groups"). This is a function gap introduced by adding the GROUPS resource type without updating this method.

Missing permission.getResourceId() filter, inconsistent with UserPermissionsV2

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission iterates returned permissions checking only the scope names, without verifying `permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId())`. The corresponding UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission does include this check. If `root.evaluatePermission(...)` ever returns a permission whose resource is not the one we are evaluating (e.g. due to policy inheritance or shared scope names across resource types), GroupPermissionsV2 would grant access based on that foreign permission. For parity with UserPermissionsV2 and to avoid potential cross-resource grants, add `if (permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId()))` around the inner scope loop.

Double semicolon on field initializer

`private final GroupRepresentation topGroup = new GroupRepresentation();;` contains a stray second semicolon. It is legal Java but is a lint-grade mistake worth fixing.

registerListener now only registers when FGAP V1 feature is enabled at startup

The previous behavior registered a ProviderEventListener unconditionally and gated the handler body with a `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` check at every event. This is functionally equivalent for static feature flags, but it is a behavioral contract change: callers that rely on registering then toggling the feature flag, or that replay events captured before the flag was disabled, will not see the old gating. Either keep registration unconditional (for runtime-toggle safety) or document the new behavior. Not a bug per se but worth a note in commit message / release notes.

The test passes, but `asn1Des != sign` and the resulting signature cannot be verified against the data. Each `test*` method should generate a key with the matching curve (P-256 for ES256, P-384 for ES384, P-521 for ES512), e.g. via `ECGenParameterSpec` and `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` initialized appropriately.

A buggy `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` that, for example, swapped r and s, added a spurious leading zero, or used the wrong tag/byte order, could still satisfy this equality. The test should additionally assert `Assert.assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and, more importantly, verify the produced signature against the data with the public key (`Signature.initVerify(...); signature.update(data); Assert.assertTrue(signature.verify(asn1Des));`). Tie-breaking by ServiceLoader iteration order is non-deterministic when orders are equal

When two providers share the same `order()` value (e.g. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200 here), `Comparator.reversed()` is stable, so the winner is whichever provider ServiceLoader happens to iterate first. JAR ordering on the classpath is not specified by the JLS, and tools/builds can produce different orders, so the chosen CryptoProvider can differ between environments with the same dependency set. This previously threw a clear error; now it silently picks an implementation. The log line also leaks a format string into `logger.debugf(builder)` (class names contain no `%` so it's safe today, but it should be `logger.debugf("%s", builder.toString())`). Either reject equal orders with an informative error, or sort by a secondary deterministic key (class name) and document the precedence.

`CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` is added only to the `create(Configuration)` overload. Although `create()` and `create(InputStream)` both delegate to `create(Configuration)` and so transitively initialize the provider, the contract of `CryptoIntegration.init` is that callers invoke it explicitly with their own classloader, and double-checked init inside `init` records the *first* classloader it sees. Three comments in this PR (cursors.py:26-27, paginator.py:179-181, paginator.py:874-878) claim that allowing negative cursor offsets is a "performance optimization" that enables "efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning" and "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". This is incorrect: a negative offset still requires walking to that position in the result set (in SQL terms it is still an OFFSET, just expressed as a negative number). The comments advertise a benefit that the change does not deliver, which is misleading to future readers and will mislead anyone trying to reason about pagination cost.

Hard KeyError on Kafka messages missing end_timestamp_precise

process_batch now constructs `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"])`. The new `end_timestamp_precise` field has no default, so any incoming ingest-spans message that omits it will raise from the consumer and stall that batch. Even if the current producer always sets it, an index lookup with no `.get(..., 0.0)` fallback is fragile for a producer/consumer pipeline where the schema can evolve. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (or a typed default) and let the new zset score handle missing/zero values gracefully.

Defensive per-segment span-count cap silently removed from the flush side

The old `_load_segment_data` aborted and dropped a segment when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, with an explicit metric/logger. That check is gone in the new version, so the only cap on segment size is now the insert-time `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua. If the insert cap is ever bypassed (older consumer version still running, manual redis writes, or a future script change), the flusher will happily scan and ship arbitrarily large segments, with corresponding memory and downstream cost. Keep the flush-side cap (or an equivalent assertion) as a defense-in-depth bound, or add a test that exercises the case where the insert-time cap is disabled.

Headline eviction behavior is not covered by any test

The stated purpose of this PR is "eviction during insert": add-buffer.lua now does `zpopmin` once the segment set exceeds 1000 entries, and `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` were rewritten around sorted sets (zadd with `end_timestamp_precise` as score, zscan returning `(member, score)`). None of the existing tests in tests/sentry/spans/ exercise either behavior - no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction cap and the score ordering, and no test verifies that the score passed to zadd survives through to the flusher. A regression in the score key, the cap, or the eviction order could ship undetected.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count() not registered in errors dataset

The SnQLFunction `upsampled_count` is only registered in the discover dataset's function_converter, but `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` emits `"upsampled_count() as count"` regardless of which dataset is being queried. When the errors dataset is used (which is the primary use case for error upsampling, and is the dataset that `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for unconditionally), the query will fail at the Snuba layer with an unknown-function error. The function must also be registered in the errors dataset's function converter.

Cache invalidation function is never called

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but no code anywhere calls it. Because the cache TTL is 60 seconds, when a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (e.g. during a rollback), that project will continue to receive upsampled `count()` results for up to 60 seconds, producing incorrect (inflated) counts in production. The docstring acknowledges that 'allowlist changes are infrequent' but does not justify serving incorrect data after removals. The cache should be invalidated synchronously when the option changes, or the option lookup itself should not be cached.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring matching despite claiming caution

The implementation does `'event.type:error' in query` (lowercased substring), and the docstring claims it was 'Reduced to only check for event.type:error to err on the side of caution.' Substring matching is the opposite of cautious: `NOT event.type:error` matches (the query excludes errors yet upsampling will be applied), `event.type:error_handled` matches (a non-error event type is treated as an error), and `message:"event.type:error occurred"` matches. This will cause `sum(sample_weight)` upsampled counts to be returned for queries that are explicitly about non-error events, corrupting customer-facing time series. The check should tokenize and parse the query (or at minimum require word boundaries / absence of a leading `NOT`).

Unrelated breaking change to user-facing error text

The error message for `topEvents <= 0` was changed from `"If topEvents needs to be at least 1"` to `"topEvents needs to be at least 1"`. This is a user-facing 400 response that has nothing to do with the PR's stated purpose (upsampled error counts). It silently changes a documented API contract, will break any tests, alerts, or downstream consumers that pattern-match the message, and should be reverted or split into a separate PR.

setUp overwrites self.user after login_as uses it

In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` and `self.authed_user = self.user` are executed before `self.user = self.create_user()`. The login and stored `authed_user` reference the parent `APITestCase`'s user, then `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user that was never logged in. The `tags` on stored events reference this new `self.user`/`self.user2` (which are different identities than the authenticated principal), so the test fixture is internally inconsistent and any tag-based filtering or permission check against the new users will not behave as intended. Reorder setUp so users are created before login_as, or stop reassigning self.user.

Organization parameter unused in allowlist check

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` accepts `organization: Organization` but never references it. The allowlist `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is treated as a single global list of project IDs with no org scoping. If two organizations share a project ID space (e.g. in tests, or in any multi-tenant view of the option), a match in the allowlist could trigger upsampling for projects in the wrong organization. Either drop the unused parameter or actually verify each project_id belongs to `organization`.

Transform only matches literal count(), misses aliased and other count variants

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact stripped/lowercased string `count()`. It will not transform `count() as total`, `count_if(...)`, `count_unique(...)`, `count_web_vitals(...)`, etc. Any aggregation that semantically counts events but isn't literal `count()` will return non-upsampled counts in the same response, producing mixed results where some y-axes are upsampled and others are not for the same time bucket. The match should also handle aliased forms and at minimum `count_if`-style aggregates for errors, or the contract should be clearly documented.

Main public function and cache invalidation are untested

The test file covers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, but never exercises the main entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss, cache-key determinism, interaction with `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and never tests `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given the cache-related concerns above, these are exactly the paths that need direct test coverage.

Hard-coded count==10 assumes undocumented sample_weight semantics

The assertions `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` rely on `sum(sample_weight)` producing 10 when `client_sample_rate` is 0.1. That is only true if the Snuba `sample_weight` column is precomputed as `1/sample_rate` rather than equal to `sample_rate`. The factory change only sets `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)`; nothing in this PR guarantees that `sample_weight` in Snuba equals `1/sample_rate`. If `sample_weight` is NULL or equals `sample_rate`, the test will silently produce wrong counts in CI and the assertion will fail or, worse, pass against a different column. Either add an explicit comment/schema check documenting the invariant, or compute the expected value from whatever mapping actually exists.

Factory silently overwrites event sample_rate with context value

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` unconditionally assigns `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever the `error_sampling` context is present. `sample_rate` is a standard SDK-provided field on events; overwriting it from a separate `error_sampling` context (which carries a different semantic — client-side reporting rate, not SDK capture rate) can corrupt downstream consumers that read `sample_rate` for ingest sampling math. It should only set the field when the event doesn't already carry a `sample_rate`, or write to a distinct field. The two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks additionally hide all errors including programming mistakes.

Cache returns truthy cached_result but stores strict booleans inconsistently

`cache.get(cache_key)` returns `cached_result` which was stored as a Python `bool` (`is_eligible`), but the return path does `return cached_result and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform(...)`. If `is_eligible` was `False`, the cached value is `False` and the short-circuit returns `False`, skipping the dataset check — this means a request whose project set is not allowlisted will never even consult the dataset/transactions filter, which is fine. However, if the cache backend ever returns a non-bool truthy value (e.g. some serializers wrap booleans), the `and` chain would produce unexpected types. More importantly, the dataset/sample_weight check is intentionally re-evaluated on every cache hit even though it has no dependency on the cached value's inputs, so the caching only saves the `options.get` and the per-project allowlist scan — but the cache key itself varies by project set, so hit rate for any given key is low. This negates the claimed performance benefit.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' uses a scope value of false but its comment claims it allows access

The new subtest primes permCache with map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': false} and the inline comment says this 'allow[s] access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. A scope map entry with value false does not represent a granted scope — the map is effectively empty for the requested resource, so it does not actually demonstrate the intended precedence (denial cache over an allowed scope). To demonstrate that the denial cache takes precedence over a granted scope, the entry should be set to true (map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': true}); otherwise the test would pass even if the permCache lookup was silently dropped from the Check path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out the exact same discrepancy in the test: the inline comment claims the cached permissions allow access, while the actual map entry sets 'dashboards:uid:dash1' to false instead of true.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache entries are never invalidated, so previously-denied resources stay denied for up to 30s after a permission grant

After a Check returns Allowed=false, the code calls s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true). Nothing in this PR (or anywhere else visible in the diff) ever calls Delete on permDenialCache, so entries only expire via the 30-second TTL. Once a (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple has been denied, the user will keep receiving Allowed=false on that exact tuple for up to 30 seconds — even after a permission grant (role assignment, dashboard share, etc.) makes them eligible. This is a regression relative to the pre-PR flow, where a re-check after a grant would consult the DB and return the updated permission; the new denial cache short-circuits that re-check. As a consequence, the same user with the same role can see inconsistent behavior: a brand-new dashboard they have never asked about returns Allowed=true (no prior denial entry), while a dashboard they queried once before the grant returns Allowed=false until the entry expires. The denial cache should be invalidated (e.g., on role/permission changes or dashboard creation/sharing) so grants take effect promptly.

Denial cache key uses raw userUID while permission cache uses the resolved UID

The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw identifier parsed from the request subject by validateSubject. The permission cache key in getCachedIdentityPermissions is built from userIdentifiers.UID, the value returned by GetUserIdentifiers. GetUserIdentifiers treats a purely-numeric userUID as a user ID and resolves it to the user's canonical UID (typically a non-numeric string). For the same user, denial cache entries therefore live under one identifier and permission cache entries under another, so the two caches never share state. Concretely, if a user is identified by numeric ID '123' the denial cache is keyed by '123', while the permission cache is keyed by the resolved UID (e.g., 'abc456'); a denial cached under '123' will never block a request that arrives with subject 'user:abc456' (and vice versa). The denial cache key should be built from the same resolved UID that the permission cache uses.

permissionCacheUsage metric conflates denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits

When the denial cache hits, Check increments permissionCacheUsage with label value 'true'. The same metric and label are used later for genuine permission-cache hits (line 132). The 'true' label therefore no longer means 'permission cache hit' — it means 'either permission cache or denial cache hit'. Existing dashboards/alerts built on this metric will silently change meaning after this PR. The denial cache hit should be recorded under a distinct metric name or a distinct label (e.g., cache='denial' vs cache='permission').

No regression test for a stale denial cache entry after a permission grant

TestService_CacheCheck covers a denial cache hit that has just been written (subtest 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry'), but it does not cover the regression scenario where a denial cache entry sits for the full 30-second window while the underlying permission is granted (e.g., via role assignment or dashboard share). Given that permDenialCache has no invalidation path anywhere in the change, a test should pin down what happens when a previously-denied Check is re-run after the DB now grants the permission; with the current code the response is still Allowed=false for up to 30 seconds, and there is no test that would catch the resulting regression.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError/TypeError if integration metadata has no 'sender'

GitHubInstallation.dispatch() compares pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. The webhook handler only writes the sender key when the webhook payload provides one, and build_integration only copies it when state.get("sender") is truthy, so pre-existing integrations (and any future flow where the webhook does not include a sender) can have no "sender" key, or a None value. Subscripting None or accessing a missing key raises TypeError/KeyError, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 to the user instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." page. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: accessing integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking if 'sender' exists in metadata, which raises a KeyError when the sender was not set.

false_positives.candidate:
Webhook signature in test_github_user_mismatch won't match the modified payload

The test mutates webhook_event["installation"]["id"] and webhook_event["sender"]["login"] and then re-serializes with json.dumps(webhook_event), but it sends the hard-coded signature sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486. The test will fail at `assert resp.status_code == 204`, the Integration record is never created, and the subsequent user-mismatch branch in GitHubInstallation is therefore never exercised. The new security check is added without a working test that proves it actually rejects a mismatched sender.

safe_urlopen to GitHub token endpoint is outside the try/except

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch(), safe_urlread and parse_qsl are wrapped in `try/except Exception` so any decode/parse failure yields an empty payload and triggers the error page. The preceding `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` call is NOT inside that try block, so any network error, DNS failure, timeout, or non-2xx from safe_urlopen propagates out of dispatch and crashes the request as a 500 instead of returning the error page. The same problem applies to the immediately following `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` call at line 434, which is also outside the try block. Both should be wrapped so all token-exchange failures produce the same user-visible error response.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 branch

The test name and the responses.replace(...status=404) suggest it is verifying the path where get_installation_info returns 404 (which should produce "The GitHub installation could not be found."). In the new flow, the first GET (with only installation_id) hits OAuthLoginView, which binds the id and redirects to GitHub OAuth without ever calling get_installation_info. The second GET uses state='ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' which cannot equal pipeline.signature, so the response is the generic state-mismatch error page ("Invalid installation request.") rather than the installation-not-found error. The build_integration 404 branch is therefore no longer covered by any test, and the renamed assertion no longer checks what the test name implies.

The new check that rejects an installation when the OAuth-authenticated GitHub login differs from integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is exactly the attack scenario this PR is designed to catch (a Sentry user trying to claim a GitHub app installation that was installed by a different GitHub identity). The branch only renders an error page and silently drops the request. A warning/error log entry containing the Sentry org, the installation_id, the authenticated login, and the recorded sender should be emitted so security teams can detect and investigate these attempts.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false; logic is dead/confusing and could be misread as a bug to be fixed later

The new function `enableSqlExpressions` reads `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches of the subsequent `if`. The function is therefore equivalent to `return false`, regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` feature toggle. This is the correct security outcome (SQL expressions are always disabled, even if an admin re-enables the feature flag, so the flag cannot be used to bring back the vulnerable code path), but the implementation is misleading: the variable is named `enabled` but actually represents the inverted/disabled state, and the feature-flag check is effectively dead code. A future maintainer who reads this as "this is broken, the last return should be true" would silently re-introduce the CVE-2024-9264 RCE/LFI path. The function should either be a single `return false` with a comment explaining the CVE-related permanent disablement, or it should make the unconditional disablement explicit (e.g., `return false // SQL Expressions permanently disabled; see CVE-2024-9264`). As written, it is both confusing and a latent footgun for a critical security control.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out the exact same flaw in the `enableSqlExpressions` function: its logic causes it to always return `false`, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions regardless of the feature flag.

false_positives.candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Incomplete double-checked locking causes redundant manifest reads and serializes dev-mode calls

After taking the RLock, the code releases it and then takes the write lock without re-checking the cache. Two consequences: (1) in non-dev mode, concurrent cold-start requests each block on the write lock and then each read the manifest file from disk; the second reader does no fast-path re-check and re-does the I/O. (2) in dev mode, every call bypasses the cache and re-reads the file, but now all dev-mode calls also serialize on the write lock instead of running in parallel as before. Adding a re-check inside the critical section (e.g. `if entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`), or replacing the RWMutex with sync.Once / atomic.Pointer[dtos.EntryPointAssets], would remove the redundant I/O and the dev-mode serialization.

There is no mutex or re-entrancy guard around srv.clean in Run, so the only thing preventing overlap was the ticker interval itself. Two concurrent cleanups performing SELECT-then-DELETE on the same annotation tables can re-introduce the very lock-contention pattern this PR is trying to eliminate, and at minimum roughly doubles steady-state database load. As written, every failure to update the unified store will be reported in the legacy Prometheus bucket, breaking alerting and SLO accounting for that label.

The previous implementation of Update first read the object from Storage, ran objInfo.UpdatedObject against that read, and then handed an updateWrapper carrying the already-transformed object to the Legacy store. The new code simply forwards the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. The legacy backend will now fetch its own old object and run UpdatedObject against a potentially different base (different RV, different UID, different defaults) than the unified store saw. The 'safe measure' requirement that the two stores stay consistent is therefore not guaranteed on Update.

Constructor docstring no longer matches the new write semantics

The comment "Mode 3 represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage and reading from Storage" implies a synchronous write to both stores. The new implementation writes to Storage first and then asynchronously to LegacyStorage, with a 10s timeout. A reader of this file will be misled about ordering, failure semantics, and which store is the source of truth.

Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled with the client

The goroutines in Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) all derive their context from the outer ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). If the HTTP client disconnects mid-request, the request context is cancelled and the in-flight legacy write is aborted, defeating the entire point of an asynchronous 'safe measure' write. The async path should use a detached context (e.g. context.Background() with its own timeout) so legacy stays in sync even when the API client has gone away.

Background legacy writers have no panic recovery and no back-pressure

Each Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection spawns a bare goroutine that talks to d.Legacy. There is no recover() guard, so a panic in the legacy backend (or in the metric recorder) will crash the process. There is also no bounded worker pool, so a burst of writes can spawn an unbounded number of goroutines all holding the request's context-derived timeouts and any captured locals.

In the Update async block, startLegacy := time.Now() runs after context.WithTimeoutCause(...) so the recorded legacy duration includes context-setup overhead. The Create and DeleteCollection goroutines place startLegacy := time.Now() before the context call, which is what the metric is meant to measure. The numbers reported in Prometheus will therefore be inconsistent across write methods.

TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection all register mock expectations on the legacy store, but the test body returns immediately after the synchronous Storage call. Because the legacy write is dispatched in a goroutine that may not have run (or even started) before the test exits, the assertions do not actually prove the legacy backend is being written to. The very behavior the PR is supposed to guarantee ('write to unified then async to legacy') is not covered by any passing assertion. The tests also do not assert that legacy is NOT called on reads (TestMode3_Get only checks storage).

Shared testify mock is accessed concurrently by the async legacy goroutine

Each test builds a single m := &mock.Mock{} and reuses it for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock. mock.Mock is not safe for concurrent access. The async legacy goroutine that the production code dispatches will record calls on the same mock while the test goroutine is checking assertions. Even where tests are extended to verify legacy calls (as recommended in the previous finding), this sharing makes any such verification racy; the production code's async write needs to be observed via a synchronous seam or its own mock, not via the same shared mock.

The Mode1 test cleanup removed a local 'p := prometheus.NewRegistry()' so that the package-level registry is reused, but TestMode3_Get still has the local shadow. This is inconsistent with the Mode1 test and obscures which registry is in use; it should be removed (or, if a per-test registry was intentionally required, the Mode1 cleanup should be reverted).

The Create comment says 'writes to LegacyStorage and Storage' and the DeleteCollection comment says 'deletes from both LegacyStorage and Storage'. The implementation now performs Storage first and Legacy asynchronously, so these comments misrepresent the ordering and the failure model (a legacy error no longer surfaces to the caller). They should be aligned with the PR description.

The legacy code had the same problem, but this is a good opportunity to either escape all regex metacharacters or split the setting on a fixed separator (e.g. `|`) and match each domain literally.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name conditional missing trailing question mark

The method at line 153 is `def include_website_name` (no `?`). ActiveModel::Serializer only recognizes `include_<attr>?` (with the question mark) as a conditional inclusion method; every other `include_*?` method in this file (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_suspend_reason?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_user_fields?`, `include_topic_post_count?`) follows that convention, and the `untrusted_attributes` / `staff_attributes` / `private_attributes` macros at the top of the file all build the method name with `?`. Because the `?` is missing here, AMS treats `website_name` as an attribute that is always serialized: when `user_profile.website` is blank, `json[:website_name]` will appear in the payload with a `nil` value instead of being omitted, and no automated test would catch it because none of the new examples exercise the blank-website case. Rename to `def include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the primary bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the trailing `?` required by ActiveModel::Serializer for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string concatenation, the core functional bug matches completely.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not gated by untrusted_attributes and leaks for TL0 users seen by anonymous

Line 43 declares `:website_name` as a regular attribute, but the implementation at line 137 derives the value from `user_profile.website`, which is gated for TL0 users via `untrusted_attributes` (see line 109). The TL0/anonymous context in the spec at lines 6–16 was not updated, and the value list at line 11 still does not include `:website_name`. Consequence: for a TL0 user whose `user_profile.website` is set, `website` itself is hidden from anonymous viewers, but the derived `website_name` (which exposes the host and, when the host matches Discourse, the URL path) is still emitted. The current `include_website_name` (without `?`) at line 153 also fails to consult `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. Add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (which will generate a properly-named `include_website_name?` that respects the TL0 restriction) instead of keeping a hand-rolled conditional.

URI(website.to_s) is parsed up to three times in website_name

Inside `website_name`, `URI(website.to_s)` is built once for `.host` on line 138 and then twice more for `.path` on lines 143, 146 and 149. Parse the URL once into a local variable and reuse it (e.g. `uri = URI(website.to_s) rescue nil; return if uri.nil? || uri.host.nil?`), which also makes the method shorter and easier to follow.

Domain comparisons are case-sensitive while URI#host is already lowercased

`URI(website.to_s).host` always returns a lowercase host (RFC 3986 §3.2.2), but the comparisons on lines 141, 144, 146 and the `ends_with?` on line 149 compare against `Discourse.current_hostname` verbatim. If an instance is configured with a mixed-case hostname (`Example.com`), a user whose website is `http://example.com/...` will not be recognized as same-domain, so the full path will not be shown even though the two hosts are equivalent per the URL spec. Normalize the instance hostname once (e.g. `discourse_host = Discourse.current_hostname.to_s.downcase`) or use case-insensitive comparison.

TL0 privacy test does not cover website_name and there is no blank-website case

The `untrusted_attributes` list at line 11 (`bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background`) was not extended with `:website_name`, so the assertion at lines 13–15 never verifies that `website_name` is excluded for a TL0 user seen by anonymous. There is also no example exercising `website_name` when `user_profile.website` is nil/blank, which is exactly where the `include_website_name` (no `?`) bug at user_serializer.rb:153 would surface — the key would be present with a `nil` value rather than being omitted. Add `website_name` to the untrusted list and add a blank-website expectation.

The sibling-subdomain branch in website_name has no test coverage

The `elsif` at user_serializer.rb:144–146 (the 'www.example.com / forum.example.com' heuristic that matches sibling subdomains with the same segment count) is reachable but not covered by any of the three new examples. The three added scenarios are (a) completely different domain, (b) identical host, and (c) subdomain via the `ends_with?` else branch — none of them exercises the segment-count branch, so a regression there would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin uses full request.referer URL

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` passes the entire referer (including path and query) as the targetOrigin. The browser uses only the origin portion of that string, but cross-origin framing and referrer-policy quirks can produce referer values that are unexpected (e.g. `null`, or some proxied form). The right thing is to compute the origin from `request.referer` in the controller (e.g. via URI) and pass only scheme://host[:port]. Also, no fallback exists when referer is blank, in which case targetOrigin is the empty string and postMessage silently fails to deliver — combined with the embed.js listener's permissive origin check this may surprise integrators.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: passing the full `request.referer` URL (including path and query) as the `targetOrigin` in `postMessage`, and both recommend passing only the origin (scheme + host + port).

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error

The closing construct is `<%- end if %>`. ERB compiles to Ruby that contains `... end if` at the end of the generated method body. `end` followed by the `if` modifier requires an expression; `end if` with nothing after the `if` (and a `%>` terminator) raises `SyntaxError: unexpected keyword_end`. The view will fail to render whenever it is compiled. Replace with `<%- end %>` (or attach a real condition to the postfix `if`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: closing an ERB block with `end if` instead of `end`, which causes a Ruby syntax error and prevents the view from rendering.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when RSS item has nil content or title

The body does `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` followed by `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing fields, and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, which crashes the job (`sidekiq_options retry: false`). A single malformed feed item aborts the entire poll, so no later items are imported either. Guard with `i.content.to_s.scrub` (or a presence check) and skip items whose title/link are blank.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` when `i.content` is nil (due to RSS feeds missing the content field) will cause a crash (NoMethodError / nil pointer exception). While their suggested fixes differ slightly (fallback to description vs `.to_s` or skipping), the underlying issue identified is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
cook_method default of 1 makes every existing post render raw markdown

The migration adds the column with `default: 1`. Post.cook_methods is defined in app/models/post.rb as `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)`, which assigns 0 to :regular and 1 to :raw_html. Post#cook returns raw when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, so every existing post in the database will, after this migration runs, have cooked == raw. The default value should be 0 so legacy posts continue to cook normally; only newly imported RSS/Readability posts (which explicitly set the option in TopicEmbed.import) should be raw_html.

Stored XSS via raw_html cook_method and RSS content

For posts whose cook_method is :raw_html, Post#cook sets cooked equal to raw. The embed view then renders the post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, which outputs the stored content as raw HTML with no escaping. The PollFeed path (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb) calls `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` before passing it into TopicEmbed.import — String#scrub only removes invalid UTF-8 bytes and does NOT strip HTML, so `<script>`, `<iframe>`, etc. from a crafted RSS feed end up stored verbatim and executed in the embed view. The Readability-based import_remote path uses a tag/attribute allow-list, but the RSS path does not. This gives an attacker who can supply a feed (or any party whose source page gets fetched by import_remote without sanitization) a stored XSS that runs in the discourse forum's embed origin.

TopicRetriever runs the full PollFeed job synchronously per retrieval

`perform_retrieve` invokes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` directly. PollFeed is meant to be a Scheduled hourly job that fetches the configured RSS feed and imports all items via TopicEmbed.import. Calling its execute synchronously inside every RetrieveTopic job means each concurrent embed retrieval triggers a full feed fetch + parse + per-item TopicEmbed.import — effectively O(N) feed polls for N concurrent retrievals. Under any non-trivial traffic this hammers the upstream feed and multiplies database writes. The scheduled recurring PollFeed should be left to sidekiq/sidetiq, or TopicRetriever should enqueue PollFeed rather than executing it on the worker thread.

PollFeed reused without distributed locking

Beyond the synchronous call, even enqueueing PollFeed per retrieval is unsafe because the job body has no distributed lock keyed on the feed URL. With sidekiq concurrency > 1, simultaneous RetrieveTopic jobs would all enqueue PollFeed and they would each import the full feed (TopicEmbed.import is idempotent per embed_url but still does N TopicEmbed.where checks). Use the `feed_key` (declared at the top of poll_feed.rb but never used) as a SETNX-based lock, or rely solely on the scheduled recurrence.

Embed iframe is created without a sandbox attribute

The iframe has no `sandbox` (or `allow-scripts`/`allow-same-origin` flags), so the embedded page can run JavaScript with full access to its origin: it can navigate the parent, open popups, send form fields, etc. Even though the embed view is intended to be simple, defense in depth requires `iframe.sandbox = 'allow-scripts allow-same-origin'` (or similar) so that a compromised embed view cannot escalate into the embedder site.

embed_url is never validated against embeddable_host

ensure_embeddable checks that `URI(request.referer).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, but the action then uses the user-supplied `embed_url` parameter to look up `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)` and, when missing, enqueues `RetrieveTopic` for `embed_url`. A caller who can spoof or sit on the embeddable host (any XSS / open redirect there) can query the controller for arbitrary embed URLs and cause RetrieveTopic jobs to fetch arbitrary remote pages reachable to the Discourse server (SSRF). At minimum the controller should reject embed_urls whose host is not embeddable_host; ideally it should compare path/host as well.

No test that imported raw_html content is sanitized against XSS

The 'works as expected with a new URL' spec only asserts cooked == raw, which actively cements the unsafe behavior. There is no regression test covering the PollFeed path or import(content containing <script>) that would have caught the stored-XSS issue. Add a fixture whose contents include `<script>alert(1)</script>` and assert the post does not render that script in embed/best.

No test for nil/missing RSS fields

The spec only checks the gating SiteSettings. There is no test for poll_feed's handling of an RSS item with no `content` or no `title`, which is what causes the NoMethodError. Add a fixture where the SimpleRSS stub returns an item whose content/title is nil and assert the job completes (or at least skips gracefully).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
downsize method is redefined, silently dropping the 4-arg overload

The patch keeps the original `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` on line 145 and then defines a second `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` on line 149. In Ruby, the later definition replaces the earlier one entirely; the first signature no longer accepts calls. Any existing caller that invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height)` (4 positional args) will now raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments`. The resize/downsize helpers are used by jobs and other models, so this is a silent breaking change. Either keep a single canonical signature and migrate all callers, or branch inside one method based on argument types.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the `downsize` method is defined twice, causing the second definition (with `dimensions`) to override the first definition (with `max_width` and `max_height`), breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size check ignores site-configured limits

`validateUploadedFile` used to read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB regardless of site settings or file type. This means admins who set a tighter limit (e.g. 3 MB) will accept up to 10 MB in the browser, only to be rejected by the server (or worse, accepted via the new auto-downsize path on the server). The client and server limits should stay aligned through the same setting.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same problem described in the golden comment: replacing `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` with a hardcoded `10 * 1024` causes client-side validation to ignore per-type site settings and diverge from server-side limits.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message reports a hardcoded 10 MB instead of configured max_image_size_kb

`displayErrorForUpload` previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the user-facing alert, so the message matched the admin-configured limit. After the change it always says 10 MB. Users whose site has a lower (or higher) configured `max_image_size_kb` will see a misleading error string, which makes support and self-service diagnosis harder.

Downsize loop may not bring the image under max_image_size_kb

The retry loop scales the image to 80% of its current dimensions up to 5 times. Five iterations of 0.8x only reduces dimensions to ~0.328x of the original, which for typical JPEG/PNG content yields a file that is often larger than 32.7% of the original size. If the input is much bigger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (e.g. 20 MB uploaded against a 1 MB limit) the loop exits with `attempt == 0` and `tempfile.size` still > the limit. `Upload.create_for` is then called with an oversized file, which either fails with a confusing error or, if server-side validation is lenient, succeeds with a file violating the configured policy. The loop should compare the actual byte size to the limit and either grow the reduction factor, use binary search on the quality/scale, or surface a clear error when the target cannot be reached.

Downsize failure is ignored, looping on the same oversized file

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns `false` (and logs an error) when ImageMagick fails, but the controller loop does not check the return value. On failure the underlying file is unchanged, so `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` stays true and the loop spins through all 5 attempts invoking `convert` again on the same broken file. The loop should break as soon as `downsize` reports failure, and ideally propagate a clear error to the user instead of silently accepting an over-limit upload.

URL download limit is hardcoded to 10 MB regardless of max_image_size_kb

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was changed to `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. This decouples the maximum downloadable remote upload from the configured `max_image_size_kb` (which can be 1 MB, 5 MB, or unlimited). On installations with a tight policy, a remote URL can now fetch up to 10 MB and then attempt to downsize; on installations that set a higher limit, downloads above the configured limit are still capped at 10 MB. Either keep using the setting (and let the downsize loop handle oversize) or document the deliberate cap.

convert_with executes a shell string built from interpolated arguments

`convert_with` runs `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``, joining instruction-array entries with spaces and passing the result to the shell. With the refactor, `dimensions` is now passed as a free-form string (e.g. `"80%"`) from `OptimizedImage.downsize`'s third argument, and the controller already passes such a string. Any future caller that forwards user-controlled content into `dimensions` (or into `from`/`to` paths) can inject shell metacharacters and achieve command execution as the Rails process. The code should use the array form (e.g. `system(*instructions, out: '/dev/null', err: '/dev/null')`) so each argument is passed directly to `execve` without a shell.

Comment claims automatic reduction 'to allowed size' but loop only shrinks by 20%

The comment '# allow users to upload large images that will be automatically reduced to allowed size' implies the file will end up under `max_image_size_kb`. As noted above, 5 iterations of 80% scaling often cannot reach the configured byte limit, so users can still hit 'file too large' rejections. The comment also conflates pixel-dimension reduction with byte-size reduction, which can mislead future maintainers. Either tighten the algorithm so the promise holds, or rephrase the comment to reflect what the loop actually does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when no TopicUser row exists

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(...)` may return nil if the current user has no TopicUser record for that topic (e.g. they have never visited it). The very next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`, which will raise `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil`. The action needs to handle the nil case, e.g. create the row or short-circuit, otherwise every unsubscribe from a never-visited topic raises a 500.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `tu` (`TopicUser.find_by`) can be nil if no TopicUser record exists, and subsequently calling methods on `tu` will raise an error (nil pointer exception / NoMethodError).

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in controller property name and template binding

The property is defined as `stopNotificiationsText` (note the doubled 'i') and is consumed by the template as `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}`. While the template still resolves because both sides share the typo, this will trip future readers and any future rename attempt. The i18n key (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`) is correctly spelled, so the property should be `stopNotificationsText`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same typo in the property name `stopNotificiationsText`, suggesting it should be `stopNotificationsText`.

false_positives.candidate:
CSRF: GET request mutates notification state

The `unsubscribe` action is wired to two GET routes (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb) and immediately mutates the user's `TopicUser.notification_level` based on `current_user.id`. Rails does not require a CSRF token for GET requests, so any logged-in user can be silently toggled off a topic by an attacker who embeds the unsubscribe URL in an image/link on a third-party site. The unsubscribe URL is also publicly linkable (no signed token), and the `before_filter :ensure_logged_in` does not help because the victim is already authenticated. This should be a POST (or require a signed token like `EmailUnsubscribeKey`), and ideally the state change should happen only after a user gesture.

No authorization / visibility check on topic

Unlike the regular `show` action, `unsubscribe` never calls `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (or any equivalent). `TopicView.new` is invoked with `current_user` but the action then loads/writes a `TopicUser` row for `params[:topic_id]` without verifying the topic exists, is not deleted, and is in a category the user is allowed to see. A user could be subscribed/muted on topics they should never have known about, and the response can leak topic state for topics in restricted categories.

Template path does not match route registration

The route map registers a top-level route `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' });` and a top-level view `views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, but the template is placed at `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`. Ember resolves templates by dasherizing the route name, so `topicUnsubscribe` looks up `templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs`, not `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` (which would belong to a nested `topic/unsubscribe` route that is not defined). The unsubscribe page will fail to render its body. Either nest the route under `topic` and move the template accordingly, or rename the template/view/controller files so the route, controller, view, and template all use the same `topicUnsubscribe` name.

Unsubscribe toggles instead of muting from email

The toggle logic (`if tu.notification_level > :regular then :regular else :muted`) is appropriate for the on-site notification dropdown, but the link in the email is built via `post.topic.unsubscribe_url` and shown as "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here". A user who is `:tracking` or `:watching` will be downgraded only to `:regular`, not muted, so the unsubscribe email doesn't actually stop notifications on the first click. Either the email link should target an endpoint that always mutes, or the toggle behavior should be reconsidered.

Bypasses TopicUser.change side effects

The action writes the new notification level with `tu.save!`, instead of using `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)`. As a result `notifications_changed_at`, `notifications_reason_id`, and the `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` message that the rest of the app relies on are skipped. The client will not refresh its notification-level badge, and auditing/debugging of why a notification level changed is lost.

No tests cover the new unsubscribe feature

The PR adds a new controller action, new routes, a new Ember route/controller/view/template, a new `Topic#unsubscribe_url` method, and includes the topic unsubscribe URL in notification emails. The only test change is adding `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to an existing example and asserting `List-Unsubscribe` is present. There are no controller specs for `TopicsController#unsubscribe` (CSRF/POST vs GET, slug redirect, nil TopicUser, permission check), no assertions that the email body actually contains the topic-specific unsubscribe link, and no assertion that `header_args['List-Unsubscribe']` carries the per-topic URL (RFC 8058). Without these the CSRF and behavior regressions above will not be caught.

List-Unsubscribe header ignores topic-specific URL

`header_args` only ever sets `List-Unsubscribe` to `<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>`, even though `@opts[:unsubscribe_url]` is now passed in from `user_notifications.rb`. Email clients use the `List-Unsubscribe` header for one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058); the topic-specific URL the PR just introduced is never used in the header, so the whole point of exposing `unsubscribe_url` to the builder is wasted for header-based unsubscribe.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override day comparison mixes local-mode and UTC-mode dayjs objects

The comparison `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is incorrect: `dayjs(date.start).add(...)` returns a Dayjs in the default (system local) timezone, so its `.format("YYYY MM DD")` is rendered in the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime = time.utc()` is explicitly in UTC mode and formats in UTC. As a result the comparison only matches when the server happens to run in UTC (or in the same offset as the override), and silently fails in any other deployment timezone, causing date overrides to be missed entirely or applied on the wrong day. Both sides must use `.tz(organizerTimeZone)` (e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format("YYYY MM DD")`), or both must be forced to UTC with `.utc()`.

The new block computes `const offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset;` and then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() / .minute()` to derive `startTime`/`endTime`. This does not produce the minute-of-day in the invitee's timezone. Worked example: override at 14:00 IST is stored as `override.start = 1970-01-01T08:30:00.000Z`. With invitee in Asia/Dhaka (+06:00) the code gives `offset = 30`, then `dayjs(08:30Z).utc().add(30m).hour() = 9`, so `startTime = 540` (09:00), i.e. slots appear at 09:00 Asia/Dhaka = 03:00 UTC. The correct value is `14:30 Asia/Dhaka = 08:30 UTC`, which would come from `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour()*60 + .minute()`. As a result, for the production data shape (UTC moment encoding the organizer's wall clock) the PR silently shifts all date-override slots by the full timezone offset between organizer and invitee (e.g. 5h30m for IST→UTC, 5h for IST→EST).

The new `$queryRaw`-based integration test in the 'getBaseConditions' describe block only exercises the `scope: 'user'` path against the real database. Org scope user list excludes users only on the org membership

`buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` derives `userIdsFromOrg` from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds({ teamIds })` where `teamIds` is `[orgId, ...childTeamIds]`. In practice this only returns users who have a membership in the org *or* one of its child teams — but anyone whose membership row points directly at the org but who has no child-team membership is still included, and conversely users who only sit on sub-teams are included. The more subtle problem is the inverse: a user who is *only* an org member via a direct org membership row with no team-level membership is included only because `orgId` is in `teamIds`. If the data ever drifts so the org itself is excluded from `teamIds` (or if the query is later changed to fetch only sub-team memberships to optimize), those users' non-team bookings will silently disappear from org-scope insights. The pre-existing object-based version had the same shape, so this is not a regression, but the SQL rewrite is a good opportunity to make the intent explicit (and to add an integration test for an org member without any sub-team membership).

The only end-to-end `$queryRaw` assertion in the suite (`expect(results).toEqual([{ id: userBooking.id }])`) verifies that *exactly one* row is returned for a user-scoped, single-eventType filter. It does not assert that (a) a booking owned by the same user on a *different* eventType is excluded, (b) a *team* booking for this user is excluded by the `teamId IS NULL` clause, or (c) that the booking row is actually selected from `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` (not just any table that happens to have an `id` column). `isOrgOwnerOrAdmin` was changed from `([MembershipRole.OWNER, MembershipRole.ADMIN] as const).includes(membership.role)` to `(membership.role === MembershipRole.OWNER || membership.role === MembershipRole.ADMIN)`. Because this single shared secret authorizes writes of OAuth credentials for arbitrary `userId` values (see below), a leaked secret enables full impersonation of any user via injected tokens. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over equal-length buffers.

Webhook allows writing OAuth tokens for any user with no per-user authorization

The endpoint authenticates the caller only via the shared `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` header; the request body supplies `userId` directly. There is no binding between caller identity and the target user (no signature of the userId, no per-user secret, no replay protection/nonce, no rate limit). Anyone in possession of the secret can therefore upsert OAuth credentials for any userId, including admin accounts, and effectively impersonate them. Because the secret is also required to be 32 bytes for AES-256, a leak is catastrophic for the instance.

findFirst + create/update upsert is racy

The handler does a `findFirst` followed by separate `update`/`create` calls rather than a single `upsert`/transaction. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same `(userId, appSlug)` can both observe `appCredential === null` and both insert, leaving duplicate `Credential` rows for the same user/app and breaking the assumption made elsewhere in the codebase (larkcalendar, office365video, webex, zoom callbacks) that there is at most one credential per `(type, appId, userId)`.

Unnecessary database round-trip before appStoreMetadata lookup

The handler queries `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug: reqBody.appSlug } })` and then immediately re-resolves the same slug against the in-memory `appStoreMetadata` map. The DB call adds latency to a public webhook and is redundant: validating against `appStoreMetadata` directly (and 404ing if absent) gives the same behaviour without hitting Postgres.

Header lookup uses env var verbatim, but Node lowercases request headers

`req.headers` in Node stores header names in lowercase. The handler looks up `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`. If an operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` to any mixed/upper-case value, the lookup is `undefined` and every request is rejected with 403, even when the secret itself is correct. The constant should be lowercased before use, or compared against `req.headers[name.toLowerCase()]`.

Salesforce refresh bypasses refreshOAuthTokens entirely

`getClient` issues the refresh POST directly to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and then runs it through `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, but it never routes through `refreshOAuthTokens`. The result is that for self-hosters that turn on `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, Salesforce refresh tokens continue to be exchanged against Salesforce directly instead of being fetched from the configured parent service – inconsistent with every other calendar/video integration modified here, and undermining the purpose of the feature for Salesforce users.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED combines two unrelated flags and yields a non-boolean

`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. With an empty string for either env var this evaluates to the empty string (or the other env var), not `false`, and downstream code uses it as a truthy check (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`) – empty string is falsy so it happens to work, but `parseRefreshTokenResponse` later does `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT)`, so the semantics depend on whether the env var is the literal `"false"`/`"0"` or empty. Coerce to a boolean explicitly and either include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` in the gate or document the partial activation mode.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` call is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }`. After loading the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status`. A caller can add guests to a CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-past booking, which will create new attendees, push them to the connected calendar, and send "guests added" emails about an event that is no longer happening. The handler must reject when the booking is not in an `ACCEPTED` (or `PENDING`) state, and ideally also when `booking.endTime < now()`.

The schema accepts an unbounded array of emails and the handler will happily create that many attendees, update the calendar, and fan out N emails. The PR adds the entire backup-code feature (login flow, display, copy/download, disabling 2FA via backup code) but the e2e test only exercises the TOTP login and TOTP‑based disable. The `// TODO: add more backup code tests` comment confirms the gap. There is no test that (a) re-logs in using a generated backup code via the `Lost access` button, (b) disables 2FA with a backup code, or (c) verifies that a used backup code can no longer authenticate. The handler does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` with no try/catch. If the stored ciphertext is corrupted, the JSON is invalid, or the encryption key was rotated without re-encrypting old values, the exception bubbles up as a 500 with no actionable error. `handleSetup` (line 77) references `formatBackupCode` inside its body, but `formatBackupCode` is declared with `const` at line 163, below the function definition. `minLength={10}` / `maxLength={11}` describe the raw character count, but the field is also visually presented as `XXXXX-XXXXX` and the server strips dashes before comparing (`replaceAll("-", "")`). The previous code `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` correctly fell back to the first destination calendar's externalId. With this change, update calls that previously succeeded now hit Google with `calendarId: undefined` and fail. The intent appears to be "pick the destination calendar for this credential", so the find should compare against `credentialId` (or the caller should pass it through), not against the already-undefined `externalCalendarId`. Team destination calendars not added when no event-type or organizer calendar exists

The event's `destinationCalendar` is set by the chain to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` is set. The subsequent line `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` uses optional chaining and silently no-ops on `null`. As a result, in the very scenario the PR is meant to fix — a COLLECTIVE event where the event-type has no destination calendar and the organizer (first host) has no destination calendar but other team members do — the team members' `destinationCalendar` values are never attached to `evt.destinationCalendar`, and `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` falls back to "the first connected calendar" instead of creating the event in each host's calendar. The push should be a normal assignment that initialises the array if needed, e.g. `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`. Also note that if `eventType.destinationCalendar` is set, pushing team members onto the same array may create duplicate references for the same DestinationCalendar record.

The deleteEvent fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` exhibits the same bug as updateEvent: when `externalCalendarId` is undefined/null, the predicate cannot match, so `calendarId` ends up `undefined` and Google receives a delete call without a `calendarId` (only the `defaultCalendarId = "primary"` ternary saves it when `calendarId` is falsy). For legacy bookings that don't store an externalCalendarId on the reference, this silently routes deletions to "primary" instead of the correct destination calendar. The fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` before this PR, and the rewrite removes that legitimate fallback without providing a working one.

For dynamic events `users` is populated from `prisma.user.findMany({ where: { username: { in: dynamicUserList } } })` with no `orderBy`, so the index-0 user may not be the organizer. If the actual organizer happens to be at index 0 they are correctly excluded (their calendar is taken from `organizerUser.destinationCalendar`), but if they are not, their `destinationCalendar` is lost from `teamDestinationCalendars` because `.slice(1)` indiscriminately cuts the first element. The exclusion should be keyed on whether the user is the organizer (e.g. by id/username), not on array index.

Inside the while loop, `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")` reassigns the local `value` variable, but the matcher continues to operate on the ORIGINAL character sequence it was bound to at construction time. On the next iteration, matcher.find() continues scanning the ORIGINAL value while value.replaceFirst(...) acts on the (already-modified) current value.
