The local DB branch goes through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential(credentialModel) which is responsible for hashing the codes before persistence, but the user-storage branch hands the plaintext list to the user storage. Any user storage provider that does not independently hash the codes (such as the test provider introduced in this PR, which stores input.getChallengeResponse() verbatim in credentialData) will keep recovery codes in plaintext, and the credential 'value' field is left empty while 'credentialData' is misused as the secret store. As a result, (a) the same recovery code can be reused on subsequent logins, (b) once all codes have been consumed the credential is never removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never added, leaving the user with an apparently infinite pool of one-time codes. true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding `int order()` as a non-default abstract method is a binary-incompatible API break

`order()` is declared without a `default` body, so every external implementation of `CryptoProvider` (third-party SPIs registered via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`) will fail to load with `NoSuchMethodError` / `AbstractMethodError` at `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` time. Before this PR such implementations would be the only ones on the classpath (no ordering needed); afterwards they are still detected by `ServiceLoader` and either shadow the bundled providers or get shadowed by them, but every call site that compiled against the old interface breaks at runtime. Either provide a sensible `default int order() { return 0; }` (or `Integer.MIN_VALUE`) so existing implementations keep working, or document this as an intentional breaking change and bump the module's major version. Without a default, downstream Keycloak extensions and forks will start crashing on startup.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility concern: adding a non-default abstract order() method to CryptoProvider can break existing implementations that do not implement it.

false_positives.candidate:
Test uses default EC key for all algorithms, masking wrong-size behavior for ES384/ES512

The constructor generates a single key with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on most JDKs produces a P-256 key (32-byte components). `ECDSAAlgorithm.ES384` and `ES512` expect 48-byte and 66-byte components respectively, but the JDK's Signature returns ~32-byte r/s for a P-256 key regardless of the requested algorithm name. `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign, 96)` then pads the 32-byte components with leading zeros to 48 bytes, and the subsequent RS->DER->RS round-trip is consistent because the same padding is applied again. The test passes, but `asn1Des != sign` and the resulting signature cannot be verified against the data. Each `test*` method should generate a key with the matching curve (P-256 for ES256, P-384 for ES384, P-521 for ES512), e.g. via `ECGenParameterSpec` and `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` initialized appropriately.

Test only verifies round-trip consistency, not absolute correctness of concatenatedRSToASN1DER

The assertion `Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2)` only proves that `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` is idempotent over its own output, which is essentially a property of the decoder. A buggy `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` that, for example, swapped r and s, added a spurious leading zero, or used the wrong tag/byte order, could still satisfy this equality. The test should additionally assert `Assert.assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des)` and, more importantly, verify the produced signature against the data with the public key (`Signature.initVerify(...); signature.update(data); Assert.assertTrue(signature.verify(asn1Des));`). Without that, a real conversion bug would not be caught.

Tie-breaking by ServiceLoader iteration order is non-deterministic when orders are equal

When two providers share the same `order()` value (e.g. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200 here), `Comparator.reversed()` is stable, so the winner is whichever provider ServiceLoader happens to iterate first. JAR ordering on the classpath is not specified by the JLS, and tools/builds can produce different orders, so the chosen CryptoProvider can differ between environments with the same dependency set. This previously threw a clear error; now it silently picks an implementation. The log line also leaks a format string into `logger.debugf(builder)` (class names contain no `%` so it's safe today, but it should be `logger.debugf("%s", builder.toString())`). Either reject equal orders with an informative error, or sort by a secondary deterministic key (class name) and document the precedence.

CryptoIntegration.init is called from create(Configuration) but not from create() / create(InputStream) entry points

`CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` is added only to the `create(Configuration)` overload. Although `create()` and `create(InputStream)` both delegate to `create(Configuration)` and so transitively initialize the provider, the contract of `CryptoIntegration.init` is that callers invoke it explicitly with their own classloader, and double-checked init inside `init` records the *first* classloader it sees. Any caller that constructed an `AuthzClient` via a non-default classloader (e.g. inside an OSGi bundle, a JEE lib isolation, or an app-server deployment that also exposes `keycloak-authz-client`) will have the choice of CryptoProvider pinned to the AuthzClient class's loader, even though a more appropriate provider exists on their loader. The init should happen in every public `create(...)` overload, or be done once eagerly in a static initializer / `ServiceLoader` lookup that does not depend on which API the user calls first.

The test was changed to add an unconditional `time.sleep(0.1)` between setting `current_drift` and `step.join()`. With `produce_to_pipe` set, the flusher now runs as a thread whose loop has a `time.sleep(1)` (defanged by the monkeypatch to `lambda _: None`) and is gated by `stopped.value` only being set in `join()`. false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes default of 1 contradicts PR goal

The CLI option defaults to 1 and the help text reads 'Defaults to 1'. With `flusher_processes=1` the flusher remains a single process handling all assigned shards, exactly matching the prior behavior and contradicting the PR description 'make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard'. The factory falls back to `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing 0 would auto-scale but the CLI default of 1 silently disables the new behavior. The default should be 0 (auto), or the help text/help should clearly indicate operators must opt in to get the multi-process behavior described.

max_processes=0 falls through to len(assigned_shards) via `or`

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy, so callers that explicitly pass 0 (a common sentinel meaning 'auto/unbounded') get silently coerced to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. While 0 is not currently exposed via the CLI default (which is 1), this is a footgun for any future caller (and for the planned 'auto' default). It also makes the check indistinguishable from `None`. Use an explicit `if max_processes is None` check.

Memory backpressure check likely over-aggregates Redis global memory

In the old single-buffer code, `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` returned one set of Redis memory stats. The new code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` and sums `used`/`available` across all of them. Because every SpansBuffer in `self.buffers` queries the same underlying Redis cluster, each call returns the same global `used`/`available` values; summing N copies multiplies the apparent memory by N. With the new default of N flushers (one per shard), the threshold would trip at roughly `max_memory_percentage / N` of real usage, causing the consumer to hard-pause way before Redis is actually full. Either aggregate once (deduplicating per Redis cluster) or change `get_memory_info` to report per-shard stats before summing.

Per-process backpressure raises on any one process, halting the consumer

The old code had a single `backpressure_since` for the lone flusher process; raising MessageRejected on that flag paused the consumer for the whole pipeline. The new code raises MessageRejected if *any* one of the per-process backpressure flags is over threshold. With the new shard-per-process layout a single hot shard can now trip backpressure and stop ingestion entirely, even when the other shards have plenty of headroom. The original code also fetched the `backpressure-seconds` option only when needed; the new code fetches it on every submit (small perf regression). Consider only signalling backpressure when *all* processes are stuck, or aggregating by Redis instance.

Dead method _create_process_for_shard defined but never called

The new code defines `def _create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` with logic that looks up which process owns a shard and restarts that process. It is never invoked from anywhere in the module (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly via `_ensure_processes_alive`). It is misleading dead code that should be removed or actually wired into per-shard restart paths.

test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify shared-process flushing works

The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that `sum(len(shards) for shards in ... ) == 4`. It does not actually send any spans through `submit()`, so the multi-process/sharing code path (round-robin shard distribution, per-shard SpansBuffer instances, per-process backpressure/health values, per-shard metric tags) is never exercised. Add a case that submits spans into shards handled by each of the two threads and asserts each produced its expected message with the correct `shard` tag.

Thread flusher not joined on shutdown when produce_to_pipe is set

In `join()`, the loop waits for `process.is_alive()` to become False and then only calls `process.terminate()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. For the test path (`produce_to_pipe is not None`), the workers are `threading.Thread` daemons, so they have no `terminate()`. The code only signals them via `stopped.value`, but the main loop may exit before the thread observes the flag (especially with the monkeypatched `time.sleep`). Daemon threads will be killed when the interpreter exits, but in-process this can leak work in-flight in Redis (e.g., `done_flush_segments` not called), leaving dangling 'flushing' segment keys. Consider an explicit thread shutdown with a small bounded wait, or document the test-only restriction.

Inner join loop ignores remaining_time after first wait

Inside `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time = deadline - time.time()` once before the `while process.is_alive()` loop, but never recomputes `deadline` inside that inner loop. After each `time.sleep(0.1)` the comparison `deadline > time.time()` is still correct (it uses absolute deadline), so the loop does terminate, but the initial `remaining_time` check is dead — it is computed and then never consulted again. Harmless but confusing; either remove the pre-check or actually use it to cap the total per-process wait.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Inside `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative integer). With the PR moving init to run unconditionally at startup with real concurrency (initWorkers > 1), the race is now reachable in normal operation. Any partial init work continues to consume backend resources (a SQL poller, an indexing goroutine) until the backend is independently stopped. `_get_partition_lock` uses a check-then-set pattern (`self.partition_locks.get(partition)` followed by `self.partition_locks.setdefault(...)`). Python randomizes string hashes per process (`PYTHONHASHSEED`), meaning the same `subscription_id` may map to a different queue index after a consumer restart. Within a single process order is preserved per queue, and Kafka offset commits ensure reprocessing starts from the right offset, so the risk of out-of-order processing is low. The PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and the description is just "Test 2", yet the diff also introduces an entirely new OptimizedCursorPaginator class (paginator.py:821) and a parallel branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint (organization_auditlogs.py:68-83) that switches to it whenever `?optimized_pagination=true` is supplied and the caller is a superuser or has global access. Inside that branch `enable_advanced_features=True` is hardcoded, so the only gates are the new query param and the role check. None of this is related to the stated purpose of the PR, there is no justification or doc for the new endpoint flag, the new paginator has no tests, and the audit-logs branch is not tested. This should be split into a separate PR with its own description, security review, and tests.

"Performance optimization" comments about negative offsets are factually wrong

Three comments in this PR (cursors.py:26-27, paginator.py:179-181, paginator.py:874-878) claim that allowing negative cursor offsets is a "performance optimization" that enables "efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning" and "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". This is incorrect: a negative offset still requires walking to that position in the result set (in SQL terms it is still an OFFSET, just expressed as a negative number). The comments advertise a benefit that the change does not deliver, which is misleading to future readers and will mislead anyone trying to reason about pagination cost.

Hard KeyError on Kafka messages missing end_timestamp_precise

process_batch now constructs `Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"])`. The new `end_timestamp_precise` field has no default, so any incoming ingest-spans message that omits it will raise from the consumer and stall that batch. Even if the current producer always sets it, an index lookup with no `.get(..., 0.0)` fallback is fragile for a producer/consumer pipeline where the schema can evolve. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` (or a typed default) and let the new zset score handle missing/zero values gracefully.

Defensive per-segment span-count cap silently removed from the flush side

The old `_load_segment_data` aborted and dropped a segment when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, with an explicit metric/logger. That check is gone in the new version, so the only cap on segment size is now the insert-time `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua. If the insert cap is ever bypassed (older consumer version still running, manual redis writes, or a future script change), the flusher will happily scan and ship arbitrarily large segments, with corresponding memory and downstream cost. Keep the flush-side cap (or an equivalent assertion) as a defense-in-depth bound, or add a test that exercises the case where the insert-time cap is disabled.

Headline eviction behavior is not covered by any test

The stated purpose of this PR is "eviction during insert": add-buffer.lua now does `zpopmin` once the segment set exceeds 1000 entries, and `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` were rewritten around sorted sets (zadd with `end_timestamp_precise` as score, zscan returning `(member, score)`). None of the existing tests in tests/sentry/spans/ exercise either behavior - no test inserts >1000 spans into a single segment to verify the eviction cap and the score ordering, and no test verifies that the score passed to zadd survives through to the flusher. A regression in the score key, the cap, or the eviction order could ship undetected.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but no code anywhere calls it. Because the cache TTL is 60 seconds, when a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (e.g. during a rollback), that project will continue to receive upsampled `count()` results for up to 60 seconds, producing incorrect (inflated) counts in production. The cache should be invalidated synchronously when the option changes, or the option lookup itself should not be cached.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring matching despite claiming caution

The implementation does `'event.type:error' in query` (lowercased substring), and the docstring claims it was 'Reduced to only check for event.type:error to err on the side of caution.' Substring matching is the opposite of cautious: `NOT event.type:error` matches (the query excludes errors yet upsampling will be applied), `event.type:error_handled` matches (a non-error event type is treated as an error), and `message:"event.type:error occurred"` matches. This will cause `sum(sample_weight)` upsampled counts to be returned for queries that are explicitly about non-error events, corrupting customer-facing time series. The check should tokenize and parse the query (or at minimum require word boundaries / absence of a leading `NOT`).

Unrelated breaking change to user-facing error text

The error message for `topEvents <= 0` was changed from `"If topEvents needs to be at least 1"` to `"topEvents needs to be at least 1"`. This is a user-facing 400 response that has nothing to do with the PR's stated purpose (upsampled error counts). It silently changes a documented API contract, will break any tests, alerts, or downstream consumers that pattern-match the message, and should be reverted or split into a separate PR.

In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` and `self.authed_user = self.user` are executed before `self.user = self.create_user()`. The login and stored `authed_user` reference the parent `APITestCase`'s user, then `self.user` is reassigned to a freshly created user that was never logged in. The `tags` on stored events reference this new `self.user`/`self.user2` (which are different identities than the authenticated principal), so the test fixture is internally inconsistent and any tag-based filtering or permission check against the new users will not behave as intended. Organization parameter unused in allowlist check

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` accepts `organization: Organization` but never references it. The allowlist `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is treated as a single global list of project IDs with no org scoping. `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact stripped/lowercased string `count()`. The assertions `assert data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10` rely on `sum(sample_weight)` producing 10 when `client_sample_rate` is 0.1. The factory change only sets `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)`; nothing in this PR guarantees that `sample_weight` in Snuba equals `1/sample_rate`. If `sample_weight` is NULL or equals `sample_rate`, the test will silently produce wrong counts in CI and the assertion will fail or, worse, pass against a different column. `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` unconditionally assigns `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever the `error_sampling` context is present. `sample_rate` is a standard SDK-provided field on events; overwriting it from a separate `error_sampling` context (which carries a different semantic — client-side reporting rate, not SDK capture rate) can corrupt downstream consumers that read `sample_rate` for ingest sampling math. If `is_eligible` was `False`, the cached value is `False` and the short-circuit returns `False`, skipping the dataset check — this means a request whose project set is not allowlisted will never even consult the dataset/transactions filter, which is fine. However, if the cache backend ever returns a non-bool truthy value (e.g. some serializers wrap booleans), the `and` chain would produce unexpected types. More importantly, the dataset/sample_weight check is intentionally re-evaluated on every cache hit even though it has no dependency on the cached value's inputs, so the caching only saves the `options.get` and the per-project allowlist scan — but the cache key itself varies by project set, so hit rate for any given key is low. Test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' uses a scope value of false but its comment claims it allows access

The new subtest primes permCache with map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': false} and the inline comment says this 'allow[s] access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. A scope map entry with value false does not represent a granted scope — the map is effectively empty for the requested resource, so it does not actually demonstrate the intended precedence (denial cache over an allowed scope). To demonstrate that the denial cache takes precedence over a granted scope, the entry should be set to true (map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': true}); otherwise the test would pass even if the permCache lookup was silently dropped from the Check path.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache entries are never invalidated, so previously-denied resources stay denied for up to 30s after a permission grant

After a Check returns Allowed=false, the code calls s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true). Nothing in this PR (or anywhere else visible in the diff) ever calls Delete on permDenialCache, so entries only expire via the 30-second TTL. Once a (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple has been denied, the user will keep receiving Allowed=false on that exact tuple for up to 30 seconds — even after a permission grant (role assignment, dashboard share, etc.) makes them eligible. This is a regression relative to the pre-PR flow, where a re-check after a grant would consult the DB and return the updated permission; the new denial cache short-circuits that re-check. As a consequence, the same user with the same role can see inconsistent behavior: a brand-new dashboard they have never asked about returns Allowed=true (no prior denial entry), while a dashboard they queried once before the grant returns Allowed=false until the entry expires. The denial cache should be invalidated (e.g., on role/permission changes or dashboard creation/sharing) so grants take effect promptly.

Denial cache key uses raw userUID while permission cache uses the resolved UID

The denial cache key is built from checkReq.UserUID, the raw identifier parsed from the request subject by validateSubject. The permission cache key in getCachedIdentityPermissions is built from userIdentifiers.UID, the value returned by GetUserIdentifiers. GetUserIdentifiers treats a purely-numeric userUID as a user ID and resolves it to the user's canonical UID (typically a non-numeric string). For the same user, denial cache entries therefore live under one identifier and permission cache entries under another, so the two caches never share state. Concretely, if a user is identified by numeric ID '123' the denial cache is keyed by '123', while the permission cache is keyed by the resolved UID (e.g., 'abc456'); a denial cached under '123' will never block a request that arrives with subject 'user:abc456' (and vice versa). The denial cache key should be built from the same resolved UID that the permission cache uses.

permissionCacheUsage metric conflates denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits

When the denial cache hits, Check increments permissionCacheUsage with label value 'true'. The same metric and label are used later for genuine permission-cache hits (line 132). The 'true' label therefore no longer means 'permission cache hit' — it means 'either permission cache or denial cache hit'. Existing dashboards/alerts built on this metric will silently change meaning after this PR. The denial cache hit should be recorded under a distinct metric name or a distinct label (e.g., cache='denial' vs cache='permission').

No regression test for a stale denial cache entry after a permission grant

TestService_CacheCheck covers a denial cache hit that has just been written (subtest 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry'), but it does not cover the regression scenario where a denial cache entry sits for the full 30-second window while the underlying permission is granted (e.g., via role assignment or dashboard share). Given that permDenialCache has no invalidation path anywhere in the change, a test should pin down what happens when a previously-denied Check is re-run after the DB now grants the permission; with the current code the response is still Allowed=false for up to 30 seconds, and there is no test that would catch the resulting regression.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker reduced below the cleanup timeout, allows overlapping runs

The ticker interval was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1, but srv.clean has a 9-minute timeout (const timeout = 9 * time.Minute). The original 10-minute interval was deliberately chosen to be longer than the timeout so that the next tick cannot fire while a cleanup is still in flight; with a 1-minute interval, if any single cleanup takes more than one minute - which is quite plausible now that each batch does a separate SELECT and DELETE rather than a single DELETE - the next call to srv.clean will be dispatched concurrently with the previous one. There is no mutex or re-entrancy guard around srv.clean in Run, so the only thing preventing overlap was the ticker interval itself. Two concurrent cleanups performing SELECT-then-DELETE on the same annotation tables can re-introduce the very lock-contention pattern this PR is trying to eliminate, and at minimum roughly doubles steady-state database load. Either keep the interval >= the cleanup timeout, lower the timeout below 1 minute, or add a guard (sync.Mutex / atomic flag) so srv.clean cannot overlap with itself.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the reduction of the cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute as a concern because it can increase database load and contention. The candidate adds overlapping cleanup runs as a specific mechanism for those risks, which is consistent with the golden comment's underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:

In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a configured batch size > 999, the IN-list is built by fmt.Sprint(ids[0]) followed by a loop of fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) for each subsequent id. Each Sprintf allocates and copies the entire growing string, making the total work O(n^2) in len(ids). The new integration test exercises exactly this path with batch size 32767 and ~32k ids, so the construction cost dominates the batch. Use strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt for an O(n) build.

deleteByIDs chooses the string-interpolated IN-list based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit rather than on len(ids). When an operator configures a batch size larger than 999 but a particular fetchIDs call returns fewer matching rows than that (e.g. near the end of cleanup, or whenever fewer annotations match the WHERE clause than the batch size), the code still falls into the O(n^2) string-interpolated path even though parameterized placeholders would be safe and faster. The branch should be conditioned on len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit so the interpolation fallback is only taken when we actually have more ids than SQLite's parameter limit.

false_positives.candidate:
Storage.Create failure is recorded as a legacy-store failure

When d.Storage.Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of d.recordStorageDuration. Metrics dashboards that alert on the 'legacy' failure label will be misled: every unified-storage Create error will be misattributed to the legacy backend. The same pattern is also wrong on the Update path (line 129).

Storage.Update failure is recorded as a legacy-store failure

On d.Storage.Update error, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). It should be d.recordStorageDuration. As written, every failure to update the unified store will be reported in the legacy Prometheus bucket, breaking alerting and SLO accounting for that label.

Legacy Update receives the raw objInfo instead of the storage-transformed object

The previous implementation of Update first read the object from Storage, ran objInfo.UpdatedObject against that read, and then handed an updateWrapper carrying the already-transformed object to the Legacy store. The new code simply forwards the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. The legacy backend will now fetch its own old object and run UpdatedObject against a potentially different base (different RV, different UID, different defaults) than the unified store saw. The 'safe measure' requirement that the two stores stay consistent is therefore not guaranteed on Update.

Constructor docstring no longer matches the new write semantics

The comment "Mode 3 represents writing to LegacyStorage and Storage and reading from Storage" implies a synchronous write to both stores. The new implementation writes to Storage first and then asynchronously to LegacyStorage, with a 10s timeout. A reader of this file will be misled about ordering, failure semantics, and which store is the source of truth.

Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled with the client

The goroutines in Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) all derive their context from the outer ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). If the HTTP client disconnects mid-request, the request context is cancelled and the in-flight legacy write is aborted, defeating the entire point of an asynchronous 'safe measure' write. The async path should use a detached context (e.g. context.Background() with its own timeout) so legacy stays in sync even when the API client has gone away.

Background legacy writers have no panic recovery and no back-pressure

Each Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection spawns a bare goroutine that talks to d.Legacy. There is no recover() guard, so a panic in the legacy backend (or in the metric recorder) will crash the process. There is also no bounded worker pool, so a burst of writes can spawn an unbounded number of goroutines all holding the request's context-derived timeouts and any captured locals.

Update async goroutine measures legacy duration after creating the timeout context

In the Update async block, startLegacy := time.Now() runs after context.WithTimeoutCause(...) so the recorded legacy duration includes context-setup overhead. The Create and DeleteCollection goroutines place startLegacy := time.Now() before the context call, which is what the metric is meant to measure. The numbers reported in Prometheus will therefore be inconsistent across write methods.

Mode 3 write tests never verify the async legacy call happened

TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection all register mock expectations on the legacy store, but the test body returns immediately after the synchronous Storage call. Because the legacy write is dispatched in a goroutine that may not have run (or even started) before the test exits, the assertions do not actually prove the legacy backend is being written to. The very behavior the PR is supposed to guarantee ('write to unified then async to legacy') is not covered by any passing assertion. The tests also do not assert that legacy is NOT called on reads (TestMode3_Get only checks storage).

Shared testify mock is accessed concurrently by the async legacy goroutine

Each test builds a single m := &mock.Mock{} and reuses it for both legacyStoreMock and storageMock. mock.Mock is not safe for concurrent access. The async legacy goroutine that the production code dispatches will record calls on the same mock while the test goroutine is checking assertions. Even where tests are extended to verify legacy calls (as recommended in the previous finding), this sharing makes any such verification racy; the production code's async write needs to be observed via a synchronous seam or its own mock, not via the same shared mock.

TestMode3_Get re-introduces the local prometheus shadow the Mode1 cleanup removed

The Mode1 test cleanup removed a local 'p := prometheus.NewRegistry()' so that the package-level registry is reused, but TestMode3_Get still has the local shadow. This is inconsistent with the Mode1 test and obscures which registry is in use; it should be removed (or, if a per-test registry was intentionally required, the Mode1 cleanup should be reverted).

Per-method comments still describe the old synchronous dual-write semantics

The Create comment says 'writes to LegacyStorage and Storage' and the DeleteCollection comment says 'deletes from both LegacyStorage and Storage'. The implementation now performs Storage first and Legacy asynchronously, so these comments misrepresent the ordering and the failure model (a legacy error no longer surfaces to the caller). They should be aligned with the PR description.

applyTemplateVariables is invoked twice for every shard-group sub-request

runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables once per query to produce the interpolated `queries` array that is then handed to splitQueriesByStreamShard. splitQueriesByStreamShard calls runSplitQuery (line 163) once per shard group, and runSplitQuery (this file line 299) again calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on the already-interpolated targets. The shard-splitting test now demonstrates this: a request with one query produces 4 shard groups, so applyTemplateVariables is invoked 5 times for the same set of targets when only 1 call is needed. applyTemplateVariables is non-trivial (it walks the template substitution pipeline, including ${var}, $var, [[var]] and built-ins like $__range/$__interval, plus ad-hoc filters), so the extra calls are wasted CPU on every sharded request and scale with the number of groups. Consider either moving the interpolation out of the per-group loop (so it happens exactly once in runShardSplitQuery) or adding an option like `skipInterpolation` to runSplitQuery so the delegation from runShardSplitQuery does not re-interpolate the already-interpolated queries.

Filter order changed: queries that interpolate to an empty expression are no longer filtered out

The new code filters `request.targets` by `query.expr` and `!query.hide` BEFORE calling applyTemplateVariables, while the previous implementation invoked `interpolateVariablesInQueries` first and then filtered. With the previous order, a target whose template variables resolved to an empty string (for example `${var}` where `var` is unset or empty, or `{label="${var}"}`) became empty after interpolation and was filtered out by the `query.expr` check. With the new order, the filter inspects the ORIGINAL, pre-interpolated expression, so those targets now pass through the filter and reach the shard splitter and ultimately the backend as malformed queries (e.g. `count_over_time([5m])` or `{label=""}`), which will error out instead of being silently skipped as before. This is a behavior regression for the small set of dashboards that rely on variable values resolving to empty.

Test pins the redundant 5x interpolation as expected behavior

The test 'Interpolates queries before running' was changed from expecting `interpolateVariablesInQueries` to be called 1 time to expecting `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` to be called 5 times. The expected count of 5 is exactly the redundant-interpolation pattern introduced by this PR (1 call in runShardSplitQuery + 1 call inside runSplitQuery for each of the 4 sub-requests). Hard-coding 5 in the assertion makes the wasteful double-interpolation the contract of the test and will silently block any future refactor that avoids re-interpolating the already-interpolated targets inside runSplitQuery. The assertion should instead verify that the queries sent to runQuery are correctly interpolated (or that interpolation is called once per distinct query), without coupling the test to the current call count.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race allows exceeding configured device limit

In CreateOrUpdateDevice the limit is enforced via a non-atomic 'SELECT COUNT(*) ... then INSERT' pattern: when s.deviceLimit > 0 the code calls CountDevices and, if count >= s.deviceLimit, routes the request to updateDevice; otherwise it falls through to the INSERT...ON CONFLICT branch. There is no row-level lock or transactional guard, so two concurrent requests for different devices (or N concurrent requests) can both observe count < limit and both succeed at INSERT, leaving the table with more than deviceLimit rows. For a feature whose stated purpose is to cap the number of devices, this race is a correctness bug: the configured limit is not actually a hard cap under concurrent traffic. Wrap the count+insert in a serializable transaction, lock a dedicated row (e.g. a 'anon_device_limit' singleton), or move the check into the database (e.g. an INSERT trigger that counts and aborts) so the check and the write are atomic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the configured limit. Both recommend transactional protection or locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache set before DB call defeats ErrDeviceLimitReached lockout

tagDeviceUI populates a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) BEFORE calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. Previously this was harmless because CreateOrUpdateDevice errors were only logged. After this PR, ErrDeviceLimitReached propagates up and causes Authenticate to deny the user (client.go returns the error). However, once that error is returned the cache entry is still in place for ~29 minutes (the cache TTL). Any retry for the same device within that window hits the cache, returns nil, and the user is silently authenticated despite the device never having been written and the limit being reached. The lockout semantics are therefore inconsistent: same device, same DB state, allowed or denied depending on cache timing. Move the cache set to AFTER a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice, or delete the cache key on error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same cache-ordering bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the entry after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing retries to bypass the device limit for the 29-minute cache TTL.

false_positives.candidate:

The new code calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, httpReqCopy, ...) inline on the auth request path and propagates the error. Every anonymous request now performs a synchronous database write (CountDevices + INSERT/UPDATE) before the auth response is returned, adding latency to every anonymous login. Worse, if the database is slow the request itself can hang because the goroutine's 2-minute timeout is gone; the request context can be canceled by the client earlier, but cannot enforce an upper bound on a hung DB. Consider keeping the tagging async (fire-and-forget or a short-lived worker) while still surfacing ErrDeviceLimitReached synchronously, or pre-computing the decision from a cached count.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit inserts device '32mdo31deeqwes', then tries to insert a NEW device 'keep' and asserts ErrDeviceLimitReached. The equally important branch of updateDevice - 'device already exists in the table, so the UPDATE affects 1 row and returns nil' - is not covered. The stated behavior ('if device limit is reached, only update devices') only holds if existing devices genuinely succeed; otherwise legitimate users of an already-registered device will be silently locked out when the limit is reached. The PR renames the 30-day window constant to anonymousDeviceExpiration in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go, and uses the same name in the new constant in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go, but pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go still defines 'const thirtyDays = 30 * 24 * time.Hour' and uses it in usageStatFn. Three copies of the same magic number (30 * 24 * time.Hour) now live in the same codebase under two different names, and changing the expiration window requires touching multiple files. Consolidate to a single exported constant (e.g. in the anonstore package) and reference it from impl.go and api.go.

The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! check is outside LOAD_MUTEX

The newly added `ensure_loaded!` does `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` outside any mutex and then calls `load_locale`, which acquires `LOAD_MUTEX`. While `load_locale` re-checks `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` under the mutex (so correctness is preserved), the outer include check is a TOCTOU pattern: multiple concurrent threads can race past it and redundantly contend on `LOAD_MUTEX`, doing duplicate Array scans and (in the worst case) holding the mutex while reading translation files. The `@loaded_locales ||= []` initialization is also unsynchronized (harmless here since both branches would assign empty arrays). Move the include check inside `LOAD_MUTEX.synchronize` (e.g., inline the load logic) to avoid wasted work under contention.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies unsynchronized lazy initialization and concurrent access to @loaded_locales, matching the golden concern, even though it downplays correctness risks and emphasizes contention.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback ensure_loaded! runs on every request

The new `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` call in `set_locale` runs for every action via the `before_filter`. It allocates a new fallback array via `FallbackLocaleList#[]` on each call and then invokes `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for each entry, which performs an unsynchronized `Array#include?` against `@loaded_locales` inside the I18n translation path. For the common case where the user locale equals the default (and `:en` is already loaded), this allocates an array and does redundant checks on a hot path that runs for every request. Consider memoizing the resolved fallback list per locale or skipping the call when all entries are known to be loaded.

New i18n fallback behavior added without any specs

The PR introduces a new `FallbackLocaleList` class with custom `[]` and `ensure_loaded!` methods, deletes the standalone `pluralization.rb` initializer, replaces the default Rails fallback chain, and changes fallback semantics for every translated string on the server — yet no test files appear in the diff. This change deserves specs covering: fallback list contents and ordering for combinations of user locale / `SiteSetting.default_locale` / `:en`; deduplication when `locale` equals the default or is itself `:en`; `ensure_loaded!` idempotency; and that translations still resolve correctly through the custom list (including missing-key fallback to English).

FallbackLocaleList extends Hash unnecessarily

`class FallbackLocaleList < Hash` inherits from Hash but the overridden `[]` never reads from Hash storage and no entries are ever written via `store=`/`[]=`. As a result, Hash methods such as `keys`, `values`, `each`, `empty?`, and `fetch` expose the empty underlying Hash state while `[]` returns a generated array — two contradictory views of the same object that will surprise future maintainers. The class also accepts only a single positional `locale`, whereas `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks#[]` accepts splat locales; if any plugin or i18n version ever passes multiple locales here it will raise `ArgumentError`. A plain class (or one whose `[]` takes `*locales`) would be both clearer and safer.

Without it, the bullet badge now sits flush at the top of `.extra-info-wrapper` instead of being offset to align with the title baseline, causing a visible vertical misalignment in the rendered topic list.

Dead float declarations remain on flex children in .contents

Lines 43-44 (`float: left` on `.login-button, button.sign-up-button`) and line 54 (`float: left` on `.icons`) still declare floats on elements whose parent `.contents` is now a flex container. In flex containers, the `float` property on children is computed but ignored, so these declarations are dead code. The same applies to the `button { float: right }` rule at topic-post.scss line 309 and `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` at topic-post.scss line 270, whose parent `.small-action` is also now a flex container. The `clear: both` at the end of `.small-action` likewise has no effect in a flex context. These declarations should be removed to avoid confusion about the actual layout mechanism.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name conditional missing trailing question mark

The method at line 153 is `def include_website_name` (no `?`). ActiveModel::Serializer only recognizes `include_<attr>?` (with the question mark) as a conditional inclusion method; every other `include_*?` method in this file (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_suspend_reason?`, `include_card_image_badge_id?`, `include_card_image_badge?`, `include_user_fields?`, `include_topic_post_count?`) follows that convention, and the `untrusted_attributes` / `staff_attributes` / `private_attributes` macros at the top of the file all build the method name with `?`. Because the `?` is missing here, AMS treats `website_name` as an attribute that is always serialized: when `user_profile.website` is blank, `json[:website_name]` will appear in the payload with a `nil` value instead of being omitted, and no automated test would catch it because none of the new examples exercise the blank-website case. Rename to `def include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional serialization. It does not mention the additional string-literal mutation concern, but directly matches the golden comment's primary issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not gated by untrusted_attributes and leaks for TL0 users seen by anonymous

Line 43 declares `:website_name` as a regular attribute, but the implementation at line 137 derives the value from `user_profile.website`, which is gated for TL0 users via `untrusted_attributes` (see line 109). The TL0/anonymous context in the spec at lines 6–16 was not updated, and the value list at line 11 still does not include `:website_name`. Consequence: for a TL0 user whose `user_profile.website` is set, `website` itself is hidden from anonymous viewers, but the derived `website_name` (which exposes the host and, when the host matches Discourse, the URL path) is still emitted. The current `include_website_name` (without `?`) at line 153 also fails to consult `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. Add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list (which will generate a properly-named `include_website_name?` that respects the TL0 restriction) instead of keeping a hand-rolled conditional.

URI(website.to_s) is parsed up to three times in website_name

Inside `website_name`, `URI(website.to_s)` is built once for `.host` on line 138 and then twice more for `.path` on lines 143, 146 and 149. Parse the URL once into a local variable and reuse it (e.g. `uri = URI(website.to_s) rescue nil; return if uri.nil? || uri.host.nil?`), which also makes the method shorter and easier to follow.

Domain comparisons are case-sensitive while URI#host is already lowercased

`URI(website.to_s).host` always returns a lowercase host (RFC 3986 §3.2.2), but the comparisons on lines 141, 144, 146 and the `ends_with?` on line 149 compare against `Discourse.current_hostname` verbatim. If an instance is configured with a mixed-case hostname (`Example.com`), a user whose website is `http://example.com/...` will not be recognized as same-domain, so the full path will not be shown even though the two hosts are equivalent per the URL spec. Normalize the instance hostname once (e.g. `discourse_host = Discourse.current_hostname.to_s.downcase`) or use case-insensitive comparison.

TL0 privacy test does not cover website_name and there is no blank-website case

The `untrusted_attributes` list at line 11 (`bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background`) was not extended with `:website_name`, so the assertion at lines 13–15 never verifies that `website_name` is excluded for a TL0 user seen by anonymous. There is also no example exercising `website_name` when `user_profile.website` is nil/blank, which is exactly where the `include_website_name` (no `?`) bug at user_serializer.rb:153 would surface — the key would be present with a `nil` value rather than being omitted. Add `website_name` to the untrusted list and add a blank-website expectation.

The sibling-subdomain branch in website_name has no test coverage

The `elsif` at user_serializer.rb:144–146 (the 'www.example.com / forum.example.com' heuristic that matches sibling subdomains with the same segment count) is reachable but not covered by any of the three new examples. The three added scenarios are (a) completely different domain, (b) identical host, and (c) subdomain via the `ends_with?` else branch — none of them exercises the segment-count branch, so a regression there would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin uses full request.referer URL

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` passes the entire referer (including path and query) as the targetOrigin. The browser uses only the origin portion of that string, but cross-origin framing and referrer-policy quirks can produce referer values that are unexpected (e.g. `null`, or some proxied form). The right thing is to compute the origin from `request.referer` in the controller (e.g. via URI) and pass only scheme://host[:port]. Also, no fallback exists when referer is blank, in which case targetOrigin is the empty string and postMessage silently fails to deliver — combined with the embed.js listener's permissive origin check this may surprise integrators.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same targetOrigin misuse: passing the full request.referer URL rather than scheme+host+port, and recommends extracting the origin. Although its explanation of browser behavior differs from the golden comment, it points to the same code issue and fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error

The closing construct is `<%- end if %>`. ERB compiles to Ruby that contains `... end if` at the end of the generated method body. `end` followed by the `if` modifier requires an expression; `end if` with nothing after the `if` (and a `%>` terminator) raises `SyntaxError: unexpected keyword_end`. The view will fail to render whenever it is compiled. Replace with `<%- end %>` (or attach a real condition to the postfix `if`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid ERB closing construct `end if` as a Ruby syntax error that prevents rendering, and recommend replacing it with `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when RSS item has nil content or title

The body does `content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` followed by `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`. SimpleRSS returns nil for missing fields, and `nil.scrub` raises NoMethodError, which crashes the job (`sidekiq_options retry: false`). A single malformed feed item aborts the entire poll, so no later items are imported either. Guard with `i.content.to_s.scrub` (or a presence check) and skip items whose title/link are blank.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: missing RSS content makes i.content nil, causing i.content.scrub to raise NoMethodError and crash processing. Its proposed fix differs from the golden description fallback, but it addresses the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
cook_method default of 1 makes every existing post render raw markdown

The migration adds the column with `default: 1`. Post.cook_methods is defined in app/models/post.rb as `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)`, which assigns 0 to :regular and 1 to :raw_html. Post#cook returns raw when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, so every existing post in the database will, after this migration runs, have cooked == raw. The default value should be 0 so legacy posts continue to cook normally; only newly imported RSS/Readability posts (which explicitly set the option in TopicEmbed.import) should be raw_html.

Stored XSS via raw_html cook_method and RSS content

For posts whose cook_method is :raw_html, Post#cook sets cooked equal to raw. The embed view then renders the post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, which outputs the stored content as raw HTML with no escaping. The PollFeed path (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb) calls `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` before passing it into TopicEmbed.import — String#scrub only removes invalid UTF-8 bytes and does NOT strip HTML, so `<script>`, `<iframe>`, etc. from a crafted RSS feed end up stored verbatim and executed in the embed view. The Readability-based import_remote path uses a tag/attribute allow-list, but the RSS path does not. This gives an attacker who can supply a feed (or any party whose source page gets fetched by import_remote without sanitization) a stored XSS that runs in the discourse forum's embed origin.

TopicRetriever runs the full PollFeed job synchronously per retrieval

`perform_retrieve` invokes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` directly. PollFeed is meant to be a Scheduled hourly job that fetches the configured RSS feed and imports all items via TopicEmbed.import. Calling its execute synchronously inside every RetrieveTopic job means each concurrent embed retrieval triggers a full feed fetch + parse + per-item TopicEmbed.import — effectively O(N) feed polls for N concurrent retrievals. Under any non-trivial traffic this hammers the upstream feed and multiplies database writes. The scheduled recurring PollFeed should be left to sidekiq/sidetiq, or TopicRetriever should enqueue PollFeed rather than executing it on the worker thread.

PollFeed reused without distributed locking

Beyond the synchronous call, even enqueueing PollFeed per retrieval is unsafe because the job body has no distributed lock keyed on the feed URL. With sidekiq concurrency > 1, simultaneous RetrieveTopic jobs would all enqueue PollFeed and they would each import the full feed (TopicEmbed.import is idempotent per embed_url but still does N TopicEmbed.where checks). Use the `feed_key` (declared at the top of poll_feed.rb but never used) as a SETNX-based lock, or rely solely on the scheduled recurrence.

Embed iframe is created without a sandbox attribute

The iframe has no `sandbox` (or `allow-scripts`/`allow-same-origin` flags), so the embedded page can run JavaScript with full access to its origin: it can navigate the parent, open popups, send form fields, etc. Even though the embed view is intended to be simple, defense in depth requires `iframe.sandbox = 'allow-scripts allow-same-origin'` (or similar) so that a compromised embed view cannot escalate into the embedder site.

embed_url is never validated against embeddable_host

ensure_embeddable checks that `URI(request.referer).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, but the action then uses the user-supplied `embed_url` parameter to look up `TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed(embed_url)` and, when missing, enqueues `RetrieveTopic` for `embed_url`. A caller who can spoof or sit on the embeddable host (any XSS / open redirect there) can query the controller for arbitrary embed URLs and cause RetrieveTopic jobs to fetch arbitrary remote pages reachable to the Discourse server (SSRF). At minimum the controller should reject embed_urls whose host is not embeddable_host; ideally it should compare path/host as well.

No test that imported raw_html content is sanitized against XSS

The 'works as expected with a new URL' spec only asserts cooked == raw, which actively cements the unsafe behavior. There is no regression test covering the PollFeed path or import(content containing <script>) that would have caught the stored-XSS issue. Add a fixture whose contents include `<script>alert(1)</script>` and assert the post does not render that script in embed/best.

No test for nil/missing RSS fields

The spec only checks the gating SiteSettings. There is no test for poll_feed's handling of an RSS item with no `content` or no `title`, which is what causes the NoMethodError. Add a fixture where the SimpleRSS stub returns an item whose content/title is nil and assert the job completes (or at least skips gracefully).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
downsize method is redefined, silently dropping the 4-arg overload

The patch keeps the original `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` on line 145 and then defines a second `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` on line 149. In Ruby, the later definition replaces the earlier one entirely; the first signature no longer accepts calls. Any existing caller that invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height)` (4 positional args) will now raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments`. The resize/downsize helpers are used by jobs and other models, so this is a silent breaking change. Either keep a single canonical signature and migrate all callers, or branch inside one method based on argument types.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the second Ruby downsize definition overrides the first, making the separate width/height signature unavailable and breaking existing callers. The candidate's specific claim about four arguments raising ArgumentError is inaccurate because the new signature accepts four arguments, but it identifies the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size check ignores site-configured limits

`validateUploadedFile` used to read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb`. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB regardless of site settings or file type. This means admins who set a tighter limit (e.g. 3 MB) will accept up to 10 MB in the browser, only to be rejected by the server (or worse, accepted via the new auto-downsize path on the server). The client and server limits should stay aligned through the same setting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: hardcoding the client upload limit to 10 * 1024 KB ignores per-type site settings and can cause client/server limit mismatches. The candidate does not mention the 413 handler, but it clearly matches the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message reports a hardcoded 10 MB instead of configured max_image_size_kb

`displayErrorForUpload` previously displayed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` in the user-facing alert, so the message matched the admin-configured limit. After the change it always says 10 MB. Users whose site has a lower (or higher) configured `max_image_size_kb` will see a misleading error string, which makes support and self-service diagnosis harder.

Downsize loop may not bring the image under max_image_size_kb

The retry loop scales the image to 80% of its current dimensions up to 5 times. Five iterations of 0.8x only reduces dimensions to ~0.328x of the original, which for typical JPEG/PNG content yields a file that is often larger than 32.7% of the original size. If the input is much bigger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (e.g. 20 MB uploaded against a 1 MB limit) the loop exits with `attempt == 0` and `tempfile.size` still > the limit. `Upload.create_for` is then called with an oversized file, which either fails with a confusing error or, if server-side validation is lenient, succeeds with a file violating the configured policy. The loop should compare the actual byte size to the limit and either grow the reduction factor, use binary search on the quality/scale, or surface a clear error when the target cannot be reached.

Downsize failure is ignored, looping on the same oversized file

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns `false` (and logs an error) when ImageMagick fails, but the controller loop does not check the return value. On failure the underlying file is unchanged, so `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` stays true and the loop spins through all 5 attempts invoking `convert` again on the same broken file. The loop should break as soon as `downsize` reports failure, and ideally propagate a clear error to the user instead of silently accepting an over-limit upload.

URL download limit is hardcoded to 10 MB regardless of max_image_size_kb

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was changed to `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. This decouples the maximum downloadable remote upload from the configured `max_image_size_kb` (which can be 1 MB, 5 MB, or unlimited). On installations with a tight policy, a remote URL can now fetch up to 10 MB and then attempt to downsize; on installations that set a higher limit, downloads above the configured limit are still capped at 10 MB. Either keep using the setting (and let the downsize loop handle oversize) or document the deliberate cap.

convert_with executes a shell string built from interpolated arguments

`convert_with` runs `` `#{instructions.join(" ")} &> /dev/null` ``, joining instruction-array entries with spaces and passing the result to the shell. With the refactor, `dimensions` is now passed as a free-form string (e.g. `"80%"`) from `OptimizedImage.downsize`'s third argument, and the controller already passes such a string. Any future caller that forwards user-controlled content into `dimensions` (or into `from`/`to` paths) can inject shell metacharacters and achieve command execution as the Rails process. The code should use the array form (e.g. `system(*instructions, out: '/dev/null', err: '/dev/null')`) so each argument is passed directly to `execve` without a shell.

Comment claims automatic reduction 'to allowed size' but loop only shrinks by 20%

The comment '# allow users to upload large images that will be automatically reduced to allowed size' implies the file will end up under `max_image_size_kb`. As noted above, 5 iterations of 80% scaling often cannot reach the configured byte limit, so users can still hit 'file too large' rejections. The comment also conflates pixel-dimension reduction with byte-size reduction, which can mislead future maintainers. Either tighten the algorithm so the promise holds, or rephrase the comment to reflect what the loop actually does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when no TopicUser row exists

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(...)` may return nil if the current user has no TopicUser record for that topic (e.g. they have never visited it). The very next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`, which will raise `NoMethodError: undefined method 'notification_level' for nil`. The action needs to handle the nil case, e.g. create the row or short-circuit, otherwise every unsubscribe from a never-visited topic raises a 500.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: TopicUser.find_by may return nil when no record exists, and calling a method on tu then raises an exception.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in controller property name and template binding

The property is defined as `stopNotificiationsText` (note the doubled 'i') and is consumed by the template as `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}`. While the template still resolves because both sides share the typo, this will trip future readers and any future rename attempt. The i18n key (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`) is correctly spelled, so the property should be `stopNotificationsText`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the misspelled property `stopNotificiationsText` and recommend renaming it to `stopNotificationsText`. The candidate's additional discussion of the template binding concerns the same underlying typo.

false_positives.candidate:
CSRF: GET request mutates notification state

The `unsubscribe` action is wired to two GET routes (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` and `get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb) and immediately mutates the user's `TopicUser.notification_level` based on `current_user.id`. Rails does not require a CSRF token for GET requests, so any logged-in user can be silently toggled off a topic by an attacker who embeds the unsubscribe URL in an image/link on a third-party site. The unsubscribe URL is also publicly linkable (no signed token), and the `before_filter :ensure_logged_in` does not help because the victim is already authenticated. This should be a POST (or require a signed token like `EmailUnsubscribeKey`), and ideally the state change should happen only after a user gesture.

No authorization / visibility check on topic

Unlike the regular `show` action, `unsubscribe` never calls `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (or any equivalent). `TopicView.new` is invoked with `current_user` but the action then loads/writes a `TopicUser` row for `params[:topic_id]` without verifying the topic exists, is not deleted, and is in a category the user is allowed to see. A user could be subscribed/muted on topics they should never have known about, and the response can leak topic state for topics in restricted categories.

Template path does not match route registration

The route map registers a top-level route `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' });` and a top-level view `views/topic-unsubscribe.js.es6`, but the template is placed at `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`. Ember resolves templates by dasherizing the route name, so `topicUnsubscribe` looks up `templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs`, not `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` (which would belong to a nested `topic/unsubscribe` route that is not defined). The unsubscribe page will fail to render its body. Either nest the route under `topic` and move the template accordingly, or rename the template/view/controller files so the route, controller, view, and template all use the same `topicUnsubscribe` name.

Unsubscribe toggles instead of muting from email

The toggle logic (`if tu.notification_level > :regular then :regular else :muted`) is appropriate for the on-site notification dropdown, but the link in the email is built via `post.topic.unsubscribe_url` and shown as "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here". A user who is `:tracking` or `:watching` will be downgraded only to `:regular`, not muted, so the unsubscribe email doesn't actually stop notifications on the first click. Either the email link should target an endpoint that always mutes, or the toggle behavior should be reconsidered.

Bypasses TopicUser.change side effects

The action writes the new notification level with `tu.save!`, instead of using `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)`. As a result `notifications_changed_at`, `notifications_reason_id`, and the `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", {notification_level_change: ...})` message that the rest of the app relies on are skipped. The client will not refresh its notification-level badge, and auditing/debugging of why a notification level changed is lost.

No tests cover the new unsubscribe feature

The PR adds a new controller action, new routes, a new Ember route/controller/view/template, a new `Topic#unsubscribe_url` method, and includes the topic unsubscribe URL in notification emails. The only test change is adding `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to an existing example and asserting `List-Unsubscribe` is present. There are no controller specs for `TopicsController#unsubscribe` (CSRF/POST vs GET, slug redirect, nil TopicUser, permission check), no assertions that the email body actually contains the topic-specific unsubscribe link, and no assertion that `header_args['List-Unsubscribe']` carries the per-topic URL (RFC 8058). Without these the CSRF and behavior regressions above will not be caught.

List-Unsubscribe header ignores topic-specific URL

`header_args` only ever sets `List-Unsubscribe` to `<#{template_args[:user_preferences_url]}>`, even though `@opts[:unsubscribe_url]` is now passed in from `user_notifications.rb`. Email clients use the `List-Unsubscribe` header for one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058); the topic-specific URL the PR just introduced is never used in the header, so the whole point of exposing `unsubscribe_url` to the builder is wasted for header-based unsubscribe.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data; @updatedAt is not bumped

The new call `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is preceded by the comment `// Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential`, but the `data` argument is an empty object. Prisma does not update any column (including `@updatedAt`) when `data` is empty, so this is effectively a no-op (or, depending on the Prisma version, throws) while pretending to refresh the timestamp. Either remove the call (the author notes the webhook handler already updates this field) or pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` so the intent matches the behavior.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that passing an empty data object to updateManyByCredentialId prevents Prisma's @updatedAt timestamp from advancing, and both suggest explicitly setting updatedAt.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
macOS-only sed -i '' syntax breaks on Linux

`sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses BSD/macOS in-place edit syntax. On GNU sed (Linux) `-i` requires an extension argument, so this either errors or creates a literal backup file named `''`. Detect the platform (e.g., `[[ "$(uname)" == "Darwin" ]] && sed -i '' ... || sed -i ...`) or use a portable approach (perl in-place, or write to a temp file and rename) so the script works for non-macOS developers and CI runners.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same portability bug: BSD/macOS sed syntax using an empty string after -i fails on Linux with GNU sed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check sets end equal to start, ignoring event length

In the newly added working-hours branch of `checkIfIsAvailable`, the local `end` variable is computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`, which is identical to `start`. The intent (from the variable names and the surrounding comment `slot is outside of working hours`) was clearly to compare the slot's end time against `workingHour.endTime`. With `end === start` the predicate reduces to `if (start < workingHour.startTime || start > workingHour.endTime)`, so any slot whose start is still within working hours is treated as available even when the booking length pushes the slot past `workingHour.endTime`. Concretely: a 60‑minute event starting at 16:30 with working hours 9:00–17:00 (the slot ends at 17:30, past the working hours) would be returned as bookable.
