After loading the booking, the handler never checks `booking.status`. A caller can add guests to a CANCELLED, REJECTED, or already-past booking, which will create new attendees, push them to the connected calendar, and send "guests added" emails about an event that is no longer happening. The handler must reject when the booking is not in an `ACCEPTED` (or `PENDING`) state, and ideally also when `booking.endTime < now()`.

On error the toast uses `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`. The handler should throw `TRPCError`s with translation-key messages (like the existing `emails_must_be_unique_valid`/`you_do_not_have_permission`), and the client should prefer `t(err.message)` only when the key exists, falling back to `unable_to_add_guests` otherwise.

The Prisma `booking` query does not select `userPrimaryEmail`, so `booking?.userPrimaryEmail ?? organizer.email` always resolves to `organizer.email`. This is unlikely to be a security issue (the booking's organizer email is also pulled from the same user record), but the misleading fallback hides the intent. If the original design is to honor the organizer's primary email for calendar invites, the field needs to be added to the `select`/`include`; otherwise the dead branch should be removed.

No upper bound on guests array length

The schema accepts an unbounded array of emails and the handler will happily create that many attendees, update the calendar, and fan out N emails. A malicious caller can submit thousands of addresses to cause resource exhaustion and email bombing. Add `z.array(...).min(1).max(N)` (with N chosen to match the event type's `seatsPerTimeSlot` / max attendees setting) and consider reusing `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` plus rate limiting.

In the backup code branch the lookup is `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` followed by `backupCodes[index] = null` and a plain `prisma.user.update` that re‑encrypts the array. Two concurrent requests that both submit the same valid backup code can both read the same index, both set it to null, and both `update` the row. The result is two authenticated sessions for one single‑use code. The lookup/mutation needs to be wrapped in a transaction with a row-level lock (or otherwise made atomic, e.g. by storing a hash plus a per-code marker) so that the second concurrent attempt fails with `IncorrectBackupCode`. true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

`backupCodesUrl` Blob is never revoked when the modal is closed

`setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` is created on setup success and only revoked when `handleSetup` is invoked again. If the user closes the dialog without going through setup a second time, the Blob URL stays alive until the page unloads, holding the plaintext backup codes in memory. false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login and backup-code disable paths have no e2e coverage

The PR adds the entire backup-code feature (login flow, display, copy/download, disabling 2FA via backup code) but the e2e test only exercises the TOTP login and TOTP‑based disable. The `// TODO: add more backup code tests` comment confirms the gap. There is no test that (a) re-logs in using a generated backup code via the `Lost access` button, (b) disables 2FA with a backup code, or (c) verifies that a used backup code can no longer authenticate. These are the core acceptance criteria for the issue and must be covered before merging.

No protection against malformed/corrupted `backupCodes` ciphertext

The handler does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` with no try/catch. If the stored ciphertext is corrupted, the JSON is invalid, or the encryption key was rotated without re-encrypting old values, the exception bubbles up as a 500 with no actionable error. The login handler in `next-auth-options.ts` has the same shape. Wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch and return `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` (or a new dedicated error) so the UI can show a sensible message and so the failure mode is not a generic 500.

Cancel handler invokes `onCancel` before resetting local state

The cancel button calls `onCancel()` and then `resetState()`. The parent is likely to hide the modal (or unmount the page) in response to `onCancel`, which can race with the second `resetState()` call and leave the component in a partially reset condition. Reverse the order: `resetState()` then `onCancel()`. The same pattern issue applies to the backup-codes close button at lines 266-269 (`onEnable()` before `resetState()`).

`formatBackupCode` is referenced before its declaration

`handleSetup` (line 77) references `formatBackupCode` inside its body, but `formatBackupCode` is declared with `const` at line 163, below the function definition. It works at runtime because `handleSetup` only runs after the component has rendered, but the order is confusing and tools that analyse temporal dead zones / eslint `no-use-before-define` will complain. Move the `formatBackupCode` definition above `handleSetup`.

Password field in disable modal is rendered without a label

The `PasswordField` is given `labelProps={{ className: "block text-sm font-medium text-default" }}` but no `label` prop, so `PasswordField` falls back to no label text and the styling from `labelProps` has nothing to attach to. Users opening the "Disable 2FA" dialog see an unlabeled text field and may not understand they must re-enter their account password. `<Label>` is not associated with the input via `htmlFor`

The `Label` element renders the `t("backup_code")` string but has no `htmlFor` attribute, while the `TextField` declares `id="backup-code"`. Screen readers will not announce them as related and clicking the label text will not focus the input. Add `htmlFor="backup-code"` to the `Label`.

`TextField` length attributes ignore the dash in the middle

`minLength={10}` / `maxLength={11}` describe the raw character count, but the field is also visually presented as `XXXXX-XXXXX` and the server strips dashes before comparing (`replaceAll("-", "")`). Users may legitimately type 11 characters including the dash and be exactly at the limit, which is fine, but the placeholder and helper text never explain that the dash is optional. Either accept input with or without the dash consistently (currently accepted on the server but the length limits are tight against the user's expectation) or document/format the input so the count is obvious. Also, `required` plus `minLength={10}` makes the HTML5 validity message "Please lengthen this text to 10 characters or more (you are currently using X characters)" which is technically wrong for the dashed form (11 with dash, 10 without). The backup-code branch then takes priority over the TOTP branch (`if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)`). Also note that if `eventType.destinationCalendar` is set, pushing team members onto the same array may create duplicate references for the same DestinationCalendar record.

Broken fallback for deleteEvent when externalCalendarId is missing

The deleteEvent fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` exhibits the same bug as updateEvent: when `externalCalendarId` is undefined/null, the predicate cannot match, so `calendarId` ends up `undefined` and Google receives a delete call without a `calendarId` (only the `defaultCalendarId = "primary"` ternary saves it when `calendarId` is falsy). For legacy bookings that don't store an externalCalendarId on the reference, this silently routes deletions to "primary" instead of the correct destination calendar. The fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` before this PR, and the rewrite removes that legitimate fallback without providing a working one.

Team members may be excluded when first user in array is not the organizer

The new `teamDestinationCalendars` is built from `users.slice(1)`, i.e. it always excludes whichever user happens to be at index 0 in the `users` array. For dynamic events `users` is populated from `prisma.user.findMany({ where: { username: { in: dynamicUserList } } })` with no `orderBy`, so the index-0 user may not be the organizer. If the actual organizer happens to be at index 0 they are correctly excluded (their calendar is taken from `organizerUser.destinationCalendar`), but if they are not, their `destinationCalendar` is lost from `teamDestinationCalendars` because `.slice(1)` indiscriminately cuts the first element. The exclusion should be keyed on whether the user is the organizer (e.g. by id/username), not on array index.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

In the recurring cancellation branch, bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... }) is used. Each iteration awaits getCalendar and calendar.deleteEvent and pushes the resolved result into apiDeletes. forEach does not await these async callbacks, so when the later Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) at line 652 runs, the array may not yet contain all the entries (or any of them). Even when entries are eventually pushed, they are the already-resolved values from `await calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`, not pending promises, so Promise.all provides no concurrency waiting. This means recurring calendar cancellations can be silently dropped and apiDeletes can be resolved before the actual deletions occur.

forEach(async) does not await calendar/video deletions before reschedule email and webhook

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... }) at line 553 starts calendar and video deletions but does not wait for them. The mutation immediately proceeds to await sendRequestRescheduleEmail (line 570) and then runs sendWebhooks via Promise.all (line 618). Recipients can receive the reschedule email and webhook while the original calendar/video event is still active. Errors from getCalendar or deleteEvent/deleteMeeting inside the async callback also become unhandled promise rejections because there is no try/catch and the forEach ignores the returned promises.

getCalendarCredentials now leaks Promise<Calendar|null> in its return values without being async

getCalendarCredentials (line 23) is still declared synchronous, but inside it calls the now-async getCalendar and stores the returned Promise<Calendar | null> in each result's `calendar` field (line 28). The only caller, getConnectedCalendars, happens to do `const calendar = await item.calendar;` so it works at runtime, but the function's signature and ReturnType no longer reflect the new shape. Any future caller that forgets to await `item.calendar` will silently get a Promise where it expects a Calendar. The function should either be marked `async`, or resolve the calendars up front with `await Promise.all(...)` before returning, so the contract matches the name.
